title: Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
The synthetic-control estimator

Donors \(j = 1, \dots, J\); weights \(w_j \geq 0\), \(\sum_j w_j = 1\)
Choose \(w\) so the weighted donors match the treated unit’s pre-period outcomes and predictors
Effect = post-period gap between treated and synthetic

title: Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
Why the constraints matter

Non-negative, sum to one → stay inside the convex hull of donors
No extrapolation
Sparse, interpretable weights: “Texas is 45% California, 32% Ohio…”
Bad pre-period fit = nothing to say. Report the pre-RMSPE.

title: Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
Inference by placebo

Reassign treatment to each donor; fit its synthetic control
Post/pre RMSPE ratio for every unit
Treated unit’s rank ÷ number of units = the \(p\)-value
Also: placebo-in-time, leave-one-out donors

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
The fixed-effects model
\[Y_{it} = \delta D_{it} + \mathbf{X}_{it}\beta + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}\]

\(u_i\): everything about unit \(i\) that does not change
It can be correlated with \(D_{it}\) however it likes
FE compares each unit to itself

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
Three implementations, one estimate

Unit dummies
Demean every variable within unit
First-difference (identical to FE when \(T = 2\))
Today we run all three and watch them agree

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
What FE needs

Strict exogeneity: \(E[\varepsilon_{it} \mid D_{i1}, \dots, D_{iT}, u_i] = 0\)
Time-varying unobservables that move with \(D\): still a problem
Feedback (today’s shock → tomorrow’s treatment): a problem
Regressors that never change within unit: absorbed, gone

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:

Sex workers charge more for unprotected sex. Compensating differential, or selection?
Panel: same provider, many clients
Pooled OLS: premium ≈ 0. Within provider: ≈ 5%.

title: Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences

The 2×2 DiD
\[\hat{\delta} = (\bar{Y}_{T,post} - \bar{Y}_{T,pre}) - (\bar{Y}_{C,post} - \bar{Y}_{C,pre})\]

As a regression: \(Y = \alpha + \beta\,\text{Treat} + \gamma\,\text{Post} + \delta\,(\text{Treat} \times \text{Post}) + e\)
Assumption: parallel trends — a counterfactual claim, untestable in the 2×2

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Last time

Matching needs CIA: observe everything that drives selection
Today: give up on that, and find a place where treatment flips for a reason that is locally arbitrary

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
The design

Running variable \(X\), cutoff \(c_0\)
Sharp: \(D = 1[X \geq c_0]\)
Fuzzy: \(P(D = 1 \mid X)\) jumps at \(c_0\)
Units just above and just below differ in \(D\) and, if nothing else jumps, in nothing else

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Identification by continuity
\[\delta_{SRD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x]\]

Assumption: \(E[Y^0 \mid X]\) and \(E[Y^1 \mid X]\) are continuous at \(c_0\)
No CIA, no need to observe confounders
Estimand is local to the cutoff

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Estimation is bias vs variance

Global polynomials: all the data, but far-away points steer the fit at the cutoff
Local linear within bandwidth \(h\): the modern default
rdrobust picks \(h\) and bias-corrects the CI
Report several; show the bandwidth curve

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Threats

Manipulation: units sort just past the cutoff → density jumps (McCrary / rddensity)
Something else at the cutoff: covariates should be smooth there
Wrong functional form: placebo cutoffs should show nothing

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Lee, Moretti & Butler (2004)

Do politicians converge to the median voter, or vote their party?
Close House elections: the party that barely won is as-good-as random
If the winner’s ADA score jumps at 50% — no convergence

title: Regression discontinuity

Naive comparison (31) vs ±2-point window (21)

rdrobust; density test

title: Regression discontinuity
text:
Takeaway

RDD trades a strong assumption everywhere (CIA) for a weak one in one place (continuity). The price is that the estimate is only about units near the cutoff — and the plot is the argument.

title: Potential outcomes
text:
Last time

DAGs say which variables to condition on
Today: the language for what we are estimating, and what randomization buys

title: Potential outcomes
text:
Potential outcomes

Each unit has \(Y_i^1\) and \(Y_i^0\); the treatment effect is \(\delta_i = Y_i^1 - Y_i^0\)
We see one: \(Y_i = D_i Y_i^1 + (1 - D_i) Y_i^0\) (the switching equation)
The other is missing. That is the fundamental problem of causal inference.

title: Potential outcomes
text:
Estimands

\(ATE = E[\delta]\)
\(ATT = E[\delta \mid D = 1]\)
\(ATU = E[\delta \mid D = 0]\)
They differ when effects are heterogeneous and treatment is selected on them

title: Potential outcomes
text:
The decomposition
\[\underbrace{E[Y \mid D=1] - E[Y \mid D=0]}_{\text{SDO}} = ATE + \underbrace{E[Y^0 \mid D=1] - E[Y^0 \mid D=0]}_{\text{selection bias}} + \underbrace{(1-\pi)(ATT - ATU)}_{\text{HTE bias}}\]

Selection bias: the treated would have done differently anyway
HTE bias: the treated gain differently from treatment
Every design in this book is a story about killing these two terms

title: Potential outcomes
text:
Randomization

\(D \perp (Y^0, Y^1)\)
Both bias terms are zero in expectation
SDO = ATE
The regression is doing no work; the design did it

title: Potential outcomes
text:
Randomization inference

Fisher’s sharp null: \(\delta_i = 0\) for every \(i\)
Under it, every missing potential outcome is known
Recompute the statistic for every possible assignment
Exact \(p\)-value, no distributional assumptions, no large-sample appeal

section: Correlation is not causation — but why not?
text:
Correlation is not causation — but why not?

People, firms and governments optimize
Observed outcomes are the result of choices made with information we do not see
So the treatment is correlated with everything that drove the choice
“Optimization makes everything endogenous”

title: Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
Price elasticity of demand

Every observed (price, quantity) is an equilibrium: supply and demand moved
Regress \(Q\) on \(P\) and you get… a mix of both curves
Philip Wright (1928): find something that shifts supply only (weather)
That is the agenda for the whole book: where does the exogenous variation come from?

title: Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
What a regression coefficient is

\(E[Y \mid X]\) is the conditional expectation function (CEF)
Regression gives the best linear approximation to the CEF, always
That is a descriptive fact. Nothing causal yet.
Causal content enters only through assumptions about \(u\): \(E[u \mid X] = 0\)

title: Why causal inference, and regression as a tool

Regression anatomy (Frisch–Waugh–Lovell)
\[\beta_1 = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(y, \tilde{x}_1)}{\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{x}_1)}, \quad \tilde{x}_1 = x_1 - \hat{E}[x_1 \mid x_2, \dots, x_k]\]

“Controlling for \(x_2\)” = using only the part of \(x_1\) that \(x_2\) cannot predict
Today we reproduce a multiple-regression coefficient this way, by hand

title: Session 8 · Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Key ideas
Event studies. With many periods, replace the single \(\text{Treat} \times \text{Post}\) with a full set of \(\text{Treat} \times \text{Year}\) interactions (omitting one reference year). The leads (pre-treatment interactions) should be near zero if parallel trends is plausible; the lags trace the dynamic effect. Passing a pre-trends test is not proof of parallel trends — the counterfactual is still unobserved — but failing it is close to disqualifying.
Placebos and triple differences. If theory says an effect should show up only for a specific group, cohort, or window, estimate the same model where it should not and demand a null. A DDD nets the placebo group’s DD out of the treated group’s DD, absorbing group-specific shocks that a plain DD would attribute to treatment.
The abortion study. Roe v. Wade legalized abortion nationally in 1973; five states had repealed their bans in 1970. Cohorts born 1971–1973 in repeal states were “treated” three years earlier than the rest of the country. If legalization reduced the share of unwanted births, those cohorts should show lower gonorrhea incidence as 15–19 year olds in 1986–1992, with the effect tracing a parabola as the treated cohort moves into and out of the age bracket. The placebo is 25–29 year olds in the same states.
Staggered adoption and TWFE. With treatment switching on at different times for different units, the TWFE coefficient is a variance-weighted average of every 2×2 DD in the data (Goodman-Bacon 2021): early vs never-treated, late vs never-treated, early vs late (before late is treated), and late vs early (after early is treated). In that last type the “control” is already treated; if effects grow over time, its trend is contaminated and the 2×2 is biased — sometimes to the wrong sign. The decomposition tells you how much weight these comparisons get.
Modern estimators. Callaway and Sant’Anna estimate each cohort-by-time ATT using only never-treated or not-yet-treated controls and aggregate them with transparent weights. Sun and Abraham do the analogous thing within an interaction-weighted event-study regression. Both avoid the forbidden comparisons; both need a clean control group.

title: Session 8 · Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Walkthrough

Step 1 — Abortion legalization: the DD event study
Black women aged 15–19; log gonorrhea rate; repeal marks the five early-repeal states. The reference year is 1985; controls and population weights follow the paper.

PythonR


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

ab = pd.read_stata("data/abortion.dta", convert_categoricals=False)
yrs = list(range(1986, 2001))
ctrl = "acc + ir + pi + alcohol + crack + poverty + income + ur"
needed = ["lnr", "totpop", "fip", "year", "repeal",
          "acc", "ir", "pi", "alcohol", "crack", "poverty", "income", "ur"]

def event_study(df):
    df = df.dropna(subset=needed).copy()
    for y in yrs:
        df[f"rep_{y}"] = ((df.year == y) & (df.repeal == 1)).astype(int)
    f = "lnr ~ " + " + ".join(f"rep_{y}" for y in yrs) + " + C(fip) + C(year) + " + ctrl
    m = smf.wls(f, data=df, weights=df.totpop).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["fip"]})
    out = pd.DataFrame({"coef": m.params[[f"rep_{y}" for y in yrs]].to_numpy(),
                        "se":   m.bse[[f"rep_{y}" for y in yrs]].to_numpy()}, index=yrs)
    return out

bf15 = ab[(ab.sex == 2) & (ab.race == 2) & (ab.age == 15)]     # black females 15–19
dd = event_study(bf15)
print(dd.round(3))

ax = dd["coef"].plot(marker="o")
ax.fill_between(dd.index, dd.coef - 1.96*dd.se, dd.coef + 1.96*dd.se, alpha=0.2)
ax.axhline(0, color="grey"); ax.axvspan(1986, 1992, alpha=0.1, color="orange")
ax.set_title("Repeal × year, black women 15–19 (ref. 1985)"); plt.show()


library(tidyverse); library(haven); library(fixest)

ab <- read_dta("data/abortion.dta")
bf15 <- ab %>% filter(sex == 2, race == 2, age == 15)

dd <- feols(lnr ~ i(year, repeal, ref = 1985) + acc + ir + pi + alcohol + crack +
              poverty + income + ur | fip + year,
            data = bf15, weights = ~totpop, cluster = ~fip)
coeftable(dd)[grepl("year::", rownames(coeftable(dd))), 1:2]
iplot(dd, main = "Repeal × year, black women 15–19 (ref. 1985)")




Coefficients ≈ −0.26, −0.34, −0.61, −0.79, −0.63, −0.55, −0.44 for 1986–1992, then shrinking to ≈ −0.3, −0.1 and hovering near zero (with wide CIs) from 1995 on. The parabola is the signature the theory predicted: effect builds as treated cohorts enter the 15–19 bracket, peaks around 1989, and fades as they age out. (fixest::i() produces the same interactions as the hand-built dummies.)



Step 2 — The placebo cohort and the DDD
Run the same event study for black women aged 25–29, who were born before legalization anywhere. Then stack both cohorts and estimate the triple difference: repeal × year × younger.

PythonR


bf25 = ab[(ab.sex == 2) & (ab.race == 2) & (ab.age == 25)]
placebo = event_study(bf25)
print(placebo.round(2))

both = ab[(ab.sex == 2) & (ab.race == 2) & (ab.age.isin([15, 25]))].dropna(subset=needed).copy()
both["younger"] = (both.age == 15).astype(int)
for y in yrs:
    both[f"rep_{y}"] = ((both.year == y) & (both.repeal == 1)).astype(int)
    both[f"ry_{y}"]  = both[f"rep_{y}"] * both.younger             # the DDD terms
    both[f"yy_{y}"]  = ((both.year == y) & (both.younger == 1)).astype(int)
both["fip_young"] = both.fip.astype(str) + "_" + both.younger.astype(str)

f = ("lnr ~ " + " + ".join(f"rep_{y}" for y in yrs) + " + " + " + ".join(f"ry_{y}" for y in yrs)
     + " + " + " + ".join(f"yy_{y}" for y in yrs) + " + C(fip_young) + C(year) + " + ctrl)
ddd = smf.wls(f, data=both, weights=both.totpop).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": both["fip"]})
print(pd.DataFrame({"coef": ddd.params[[f"ry_{y}" for y in yrs]].to_numpy(),
                    "se":   ddd.bse[[f"ry_{y}" for y in yrs]].to_numpy()}, index=yrs).round(3))


bf25 <- ab %>% filter(sex == 2, race == 2, age == 25)
placebo <- feols(lnr ~ i(year, repeal, ref = 1985) + acc + ir + pi + alcohol + crack +
                   poverty + income + ur | fip + year,
                 data = bf25, weights = ~totpop, cluster = ~fip)
iplot(placebo, main = "Placebo: black women 25–29")

both <- ab %>% filter(sex == 2, race == 2, age %in% c(15, 25)) %>%
  mutate(younger = as.integer(age == 15), fip_young = paste(fip, younger))
ddd <- feols(lnr ~ i(year, repeal, ref = 1985) + i(year, repeal * younger, ref = 1985) +
               i(year, younger, ref = 1985) + acc + ir + pi + alcohol + crack +
               poverty + income + ur | fip_young + year,
             data = both, weights = ~totpop, cluster = ~fip)
iplot(ddd, i.select = 2, main = "DDD: repeal × year × younger")




The 25–29 placebo shows no parabola in 1986–1989 (coefficients of about +0.2, +0.2, 0, −0.2 with SEs around 0.2–0.3). The DDD coefficients are ≈ −0.36, −0.41, −0.44, −0.33 for 1986–1989, then ≈ −0.09 in 1990 and statistically zero thereafter. The treated-cohort effect survives netting out whatever happened to older women in the same states.



Step 3 — Castle doctrine: TWFE with staggered adoption
States adopted “stand your ground” laws between 2005 and 2010. The book’s regression: log homicide rate on post, state and year fixed effects, population weights, clustered by state.

PythonR


castle = pd.read_stata("data/castle.dta", convert_categoricals=False)
cs = castle.dropna(subset=["l_homicide", "post", "popwt", "sid", "year"])
twfe = smf.wls("l_homicide ~ post + C(sid) + C(year)", data=cs, weights=cs.popwt)\
          .fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": cs["sid"]})
print("TWFE post:", twfe.params["post"].round(4), " SE", twfe.bse["post"].round(4))

# adoption timing
castle["D"] = (castle.post > 0).astype(int)
first = castle[castle.D == 1].groupby("sid").year.min()
castle["g"] = castle.sid.map(first).fillna(0).astype(int)
print(castle.groupby("g").sid.nunique())


castle <- read_dta("data/castle.dta")
twfe <- feols(l_homicide ~ post | sid + year, data = castle, weights = ~popwt, cluster = ~sid)
coeftable(twfe)

castle <- castle %>% group_by(sid) %>%
  mutate(g = if (any(post > 0)) min(year[post > 0]) else 0) %>% ungroup()
count(distinct(castle, sid, g), g)




post ≈ 0.076 (SE 0.035): castle-doctrine laws are associated with about 8% more homicides. Adoption timing: 29 never-treated states, 1 in 2006, 13 in 2007, 4 in 2008, 2 in 2009, 1 in 2010. (post is fractional in adoption years; D is its binary version for the decomposition.)



Step 4 — Decompose the TWFE estimate into its 2×2s
The exact Goodman-Bacon decomposition needs a balanced panel, a binary treatment and no weights, so this step uses the unweighted binary version. In R, bacondecomp does it in one line; in Python we compute the 2×2 estimates and their weights by hand from the paper’s formulas.

PythonR


years = sorted(castle.year.unique())
base = smf.ols("l_homicide ~ D + C(sid) + C(year)", data=castle).fit()
print("unweighted binary TWFE:", base.params["D"].round(4))

n    = castle.groupby("g").sid.nunique() / castle.sid.nunique()        # group shares
Dbar = {g: (np.array(years) >= g).mean() if g > 0 else 0 for g in n.index}  # share of periods treated

def dd_2x2(sub):
    """TWFE on a two-group subsample = the 2x2 DD for that comparison."""
    s = sub.copy()
    for v in ["D", "l_homicide"]:
        s[v + "_t"] = s[v] - s.groupby("sid")[v].transform("mean") - s.groupby("year")[v].transform("mean") + s[v].mean()
    return (s.D_t * s.l_homicide_t).sum() / (s.D_t ** 2).sum()

rows = []
G = [g for g in n.index if g > 0]
for k in G:
    rows.append((k, "never-treated", dd_2x2(castle[castle.g.isin([k, 0])]),
                 n[k] * n[0] * Dbar[k] * (1 - Dbar[k])))
    for l in G:
        if l <= k: continue
        nkl = n[k] / (n[k] + n[l])
        # k treated earlier; l (not yet treated) is the control in years before l adopts
        s_kl = ((n[k] + n[l]) * (1 - Dbar[l]))**2 * nkl * (1 - nkl) * (Dbar[k] - Dbar[l]) / (1 - Dbar[l]) * (1 - Dbar[k]) / (1 - Dbar[l])
        rows.append((k, f"later-treated ({l}) as control", dd_2x2(castle[castle.g.isin([k, l]) & (castle.year < l)]), s_kl))
        # l treated later; k (already treated) is the control in years from k's adoption on
        s_lk = ((n[k] + n[l]) * Dbar[k])**2 * nkl * (1 - nkl) * Dbar[l] / Dbar[k] * (Dbar[k] - Dbar[l]) / Dbar[k]
        rows.append((l, f"earlier-treated ({k}) as control", dd_2x2(castle[castle.g.isin([k, l]) & (castle.year >= k)]), s_lk))

bacon = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["treated", "control", "dd", "s"])
bacon["weight"] = bacon.s / bacon.s.sum()
bacon["type"] = bacon.control.str.split(" ").str[0]
print(bacon.sort_values("weight", ascending=False).head(8).round(3))
print("weighted sum of 2x2s:", (bacon.weight * bacon.dd).sum().round(4))
print(bacon.groupby("type").apply(lambda x: pd.Series({"weight": x.weight.sum(),
                                                       "avg_dd": (x.weight * x.dd).sum() / x.weight.sum()})).round(3))


library(bacondecomp)
castle <- mutate(castle, D = as.integer(post > 0))
bd <- bacon(l_homicide ~ D, data = castle, id_var = "sid", time_var = "year")
# prints the weight and average estimate by comparison type
bd %>% group_by(type) %>% summarise(weight = sum(weight), avg_est = weighted.mean(estimate, weight))
ggplot(bd, aes(weight, estimate, shape = type, colour = type)) + geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = sum(bd$estimate * bd$weight)) + theme_minimal()




Unweighted binary TWFE ≈ 0.069, and the weighted sum of the 25 two-by-twos reproduces it exactly. About 90% of the weight is on treated-vs-never-treated comparisons (average 2×2 ≈ 0.078); 8% on “later-treated as control” (average ≈ −0.03); and 2% on the forbidden “earlier-treated as control” comparisons (≈ 0.05). With 29 never-treated states the TWFE estimate is safe here. That is a property of this dataset, not of TWFE.



Step 5 — A modern estimator

PythonR


# Option A: an event study in event time, with never-treated states as the pure controls
cs2 = castle.copy()
cs2["rel"] = (cs2.year - cs2.g).clip(-5, 4)          # event time, binned at the ends
for k in range(-5, 5):
    if k == -1: continue                              # reference period
    cs2[f"ev_{'m' if k < 0 else 'p'}{abs(k)}"] = ((cs2.g > 0) & (cs2.rel == k)).astype(int)
ev = [c for c in cs2.columns if c.startswith("ev_")]
es = smf.wls("l_homicide ~ " + " + ".join(ev) + " + C(sid) + C(year)", data=cs2, weights=cs2.popwt)\
        .fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": cs2["sid"]})
print(pd.DataFrame({"coef": es.params[ev], "se": es.bse[ev]}).round(3))

# Option B: Callaway–Sant'Anna via the `csdid` or `differences` packages (pip install differences)
# from differences import ATTgt
# att = ATTgt(data=castle.set_index(["sid", "year"]), cohort_name="g").fit(formula="l_homicide")
# att.aggregate("event")


library(did)
castle_cs <- castle %>% mutate(g_cs = ifelse(g == 0, 0, g))
att <- att_gt(yname = "l_homicide", tname = "year", idname = "sid", gname = "g_cs",
              data = castle_cs, control_group = "nevertreated", weightsname = "popwt")
es <- aggte(att, type = "dynamic", min_e = -5, max_e = 4)
summary(es); ggdid(es)
aggte(att, type = "simple")




The event-study leads are ≈ 0.00, 0.01, −0.01, −0.05 (SEs ≈ 0.04): flat. The lags are ≈ 0.08, 0.07, 0.06, 0.04, 0.10 for event years 0–4, each with SE 0.03–0.07. Callaway–Sant’Anna’s simple aggregate ATT comes out close to the TWFE number, as the Bacon decomposition predicted. The point of running it is not a different answer here; it is that you would have known if TWFE had gone wrong.

text:
Exercises

Reference year. Re-run Step 1 with 1990 as the omitted year instead of 1985. The coefficients change; the figure’s shape does not. Explain precisely what each coefficient now measures and why the pre-period “pre-trends test” is now meaningless.
Break TWFE. Simulate 40 units × 10 periods with two cohorts treated at \(t = 4\) and \(t = 7\), no never-treated units, and an effect that grows by 0.5 per period after adoption. Estimate TWFE and the Bacon decomposition. Then add 20 never-treated units and repeat. Report what happens to the “earlier-treated as control” weight and the sign of the TWFE estimate.
Placebo outcome. Castle-doctrine laws should not affect, say, larceny (l_larceny) or motor-vehicle theft (l_motor) through self-defense incentives. Run the Step 3 TWFE on those outcomes. What do you find, and how does it bear on the parallel-trends assumption for homicide?

title: Session 8 · Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. Each coefficient is now the repeal-vs-Roe gap in year \(t\) relative to the gap in 1990. Since 1990 is mid-treatment, the “pre-period” coefficients for 1986–1989 are differences between two treated years and no longer test for differential pre-trends; the only clean reference is a year before anyone was treated.
2. With no never-treated units and growing effects, the late-vs-early comparisons receive substantial weight and have negative 2×2 estimates (the early cohort’s growing effect is differenced out as a “trend”); TWFE badly understates the true average effect (in the simulation below the true average effect among treated observations is 1.5, TWFE gives ≈ 0.35 with no never-treated units) and can flip sign when the dynamic is steep. Adding 20 never-treated units pulls TWFE to ≈ 0.9 — better, still biased, because the forbidden comparisons still get weight; a Callaway–Sant’Anna aggregate would recover 1.5.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def panel(n_never):
    units = [(i, 4) for i in range(20)] + [(i, 7) for i in range(20, 40)] + [(i, 0) for i in range(40, 40 + n_never)]
    rows = [(i, g, t, (g > 0 and t >= g) * (t - g + 1) * 0.5 + rng.normal()) for i, g in units for t in range(10)]
    df = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["sid", "g", "year", "l_homicide"])
    df["D"] = ((df.g > 0) & (df.year >= df.g)).astype(int)
    return df
for n_never in [0, 20]:
    df = panel(n_never)
    print(n_never, smf.ols("l_homicide ~ D + C(sid) + C(year)", df).fit().params["D"].round(3))
# then re-run the Step 4 decomposition on `df`
3. l_larceny: ≈ 0.00 (SE 0.015); l_motor: ≈ 0.04 (SE 0.05). Both small and insignificant. That supports the claim that adopting states were not simply on a different crime trajectory; it does not prove parallel trends for homicide, but it rules out one broad alternative.

Facilitator notes






Facilitator notes (click to expand)





The event-study figure is the deliverable. Make sure every participant can produce Step 1’s plot and read it: leads, reference year, dynamics, confidence band. Everything in modern DiD is a conversation about that picture.
Misconception: flat pre-trends prove parallel trends. They make it more plausible. The counterfactual post-period trend is unobserved, full stop. Use the DDD to show what further evidence looks like.
Misconception: TWFE is “wrong.” It is a weighted average with weights you did not choose. With a big never-treated group it is fine (Step 4). Without one, it can be badly wrong (Exercise 2). The decomposition is how you tell.
On the Python decomposition. It follows Goodman-Bacon (2021) Theorem 1 and reproduces the TWFE coefficient to four decimals; that equality is the check that the code is right. It assumes a balanced panel, binary treatment and no weights, which is why Step 4 switches to the unweighted D.
If running short. Do Steps 1, 3 and 4; assign Step 2 as the first exercise.
Discussion prompts. (a) In the abortion study, what would a SUTVA violation look like, and why does it argue for 25–29 rather than 20–24 as the placebo? (b) Why can Callaway–Sant’Anna not help you if every unit is eventually treated at nearly the same time?
Bridge to next session. DiD needs a control group whose trend you trust. Synthetic control builds one — a weighted combination of donors chosen to match the treated unit’s pre-period — and makes inference by placebo.

title: Session 6 · Instrumental variables
text:
Key ideas
The problem IV solves. \(Y = \alpha + \delta D + u\) with \(\mathrm{Cov}(D, u) \neq 0\). Regression cannot recover \(\delta\). But if some instrument \(Z\) moves \(D\) and is otherwise unrelated to \(Y\), then the only reason \(Y\) moves with \(Z\) is through \(D\), so \[\delta_{IV} = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(Z, Y)}{\mathrm{Cov}(Z, D)} = \frac{\text{reduced form}}{\text{first stage}}.\]
The conditions. Relevance: \(Z\) predicts \(D\) (testable; look at the first-stage F). Exclusion: \(Z\) affects \(Y\) only through \(D\) (untestable; argued from the DAG). Independence: \(Z\) is as good as random with respect to \(u\) (untestable). Philip Wright’s 1928 appendix is the origin story: identify a demand curve with a supply shifter (weather) that does not enter demand.
2SLS. Regress \(D\) on \(Z\) and covariates, take the fitted values \(\hat{D}\), regress \(Y\) on \(\hat{D}\) and the same covariates. The second-stage SEs must account for the first stage; use a proper IV routine, not two lm calls.
Weak instruments. When the first stage is weak, 2SLS is biased toward OLS and its sampling distribution is badly behaved. The rule of thumb is first-stage F above 10 for one endogenous regressor; the modern advice is to report it, prefer just-identified models, and be nervous below 20.
LATE. With heterogeneous effects, IV identifies the average effect for compliers — units whose treatment is moved by the instrument — under monotonicity (no defiers). Different instruments identify different LATEs for the same treatment. The judge-leniency design makes this vivid: the compliers are defendants who would be detained by a strict judge and released by a lenient one.

title: Session 6 · Instrumental variables
text:
Walkthrough

Step 1 — Card (1995): OLS returns to schooling

PythonR


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from linearmodels.iv import IV2SLS

card = pd.read_stata("data/card.dta")
ctrl = "exper + black + south + married + smsa"

ols = smf.ols(f"lwage ~ educ + {ctrl}", data=card).fit()
print("OLS return to a year of schooling:", ols.params["educ"].round(4))


library(tidyverse); library(haven); library(estimatr); library(ivreg)

card <- read_dta("data/card.dta")
ols <- lm(lwage ~ educ + exper + black + south + married + smsa, data = card)
coef(ols)["educ"]




≈ 0.071: a 7.1% wage premium per year of schooling. Ability bias says this is too high; measurement error in schooling says too low. The book’s reason for IV is that we do not know which dominates.



Step 2 — First stage: growing up near a four-year college

PythonR


fs = smf.ols(f"educ ~ nearc4 + {ctrl}", data=card).fit()
print("first stage:", fs.params["nearc4"].round(3), " t =", (fs.params["nearc4"] / fs.bse["nearc4"]).round(2))

rf = smf.ols(f"lwage ~ nearc4 + {ctrl}", data=card).fit()
print("reduced form:", rf.params["nearc4"].round(4))
print("Wald ratio:", (rf.params["nearc4"] / fs.params["nearc4"]).round(4))


fs <- lm(educ ~ nearc4 + exper + black + south + married + smsa, data = card)
rf <- lm(lwage ~ nearc4 + exper + black + south + married + smsa, data = card)
coef(fs)["nearc4"]; coef(rf)["nearc4"]
coef(rf)["nearc4"] / coef(fs)["nearc4"]




First stage ≈ 0.33 more years of schooling for those near a college, \(t ≈ 4\) (F ≈ 16: not weak, not strong). Reduced form ≈ 0.04 log points. Their ratio, ≈ 0.12, is the IV estimate before any software. Ask the room: what is the exclusion restriction here, and what violates it? (Proximity correlates with urban labor markets; that is why smsa is in the model.)



Step 3 — 2SLS with proper standard errors

PythonR


cc = card.dropna(subset=["lwage", "educ", "exper", "black", "south", "married", "smsa", "nearc4"])
iv = IV2SLS.from_formula(f"lwage ~ 1 + {ctrl} + [educ ~ nearc4]", data=cc).fit(cov_type="robust")
print(iv.summary.tables[1])
print(iv.first_stage.diagnostics[["f.stat", "partial.rsquared"]])


iv <- ivreg(lwage ~ educ + exper + black + south + married + smsa |
              nearc4 + exper + black + south + married + smsa, data = card)
summary(iv, diagnostics = TRUE)




2SLS educ ≈ 0.124 (SE ≈ 0.05), versus OLS 0.071. The IV estimate is larger, which the book reads as evidence that measurement error and the LATE population (people on the margin of attending because a college was nearby) matter more than ability bias. The 95% CI runs roughly 0.03 to 0.22: honest, and wide.



Step 4 — Judge leniency as an instrument (Stevenson 2018)
Defendants are quasi-randomly assigned to magistrates who differ in how often they set bail the defendant cannot pay. Judge indicators instrument for pretrial detention (jail3), and the outcome is whether the defendant is found guilty.

PythonR


# Large file: download once from the book's repo
url = "https://github.com/scunning1975/mixtape/raw/master/judge_fe.dta"
judge = pd.read_stata(url)        # or pd.read_stata("data/judge_fe.dta") if you saved it

controls = ("white + age + male + black + possess + robbery + DUI1st + aggAss + drugSell "
            "+ fel + mis + threePriors + F1 + F2 + F3 + M1 + M2 + M3 "
            "+ day + day2 + day3 + t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 + t5")
# `sum` and `t6` are dropped: they are linear combinations of the other controls,
# and one judge dummy is dropped because the eight sum to one.
judges = " + ".join(f"judge_pre_{i}" for i in range(1, 8))

ols = smf.ols(f"guilt ~ jail3 + {controls}", data=judge).fit()
iv  = IV2SLS.from_formula(f"guilt ~ 1 + {controls} + [jail3 ~ {judges}]", data=judge).fit(cov_type="robust")
print("OLS  jail3:", ols.params["jail3"].round(3), " SE", ols.bse["jail3"].round(3))
print("2SLS jail3:", iv.params["jail3"].round(3),  " SE", iv.std_errors["jail3"].round(3))
print(iv.first_stage.diagnostics[["f.stat"]])


judge <- read_dta("https://github.com/scunning1975/mixtape/raw/master/judge_fe.dta")

ctrl <- ~ white + age + male + black + possess + robbery + DUI1st + aggAss + drugSell +
  fel + mis + sum + threePriors + F1 + F2 + F3 + M1 + M2 + M3 + day + day2 + day3 +
  t1 + t2 + t3 + t4 + t5 + t6
judges <- paste0("judge_pre_", 1:8, collapse = " + ")

ols <- lm(update(ctrl, guilt ~ jail3 + .), data = judge)
iv  <- ivreg(as.formula(paste("guilt ~ jail3 +", as.character(ctrl)[2],
                              "|", judges, "+", as.character(ctrl)[2])), data = judge)
coef(ols)["jail3"]; coef(iv)["jail3"]
# R drops collinear terms automatically; Python's linearmodels does not, hence the trimmed list above.




OLS: detention raises the probability of a guilty finding by ≈ 0.035 (3.5 points). 2SLS: ≈ 0.16 (SE ≈ 0.07) — more than four times larger. The first-stage F is in the hundreds. Interpretation: for defendants whose detention depends on which judge they drew, being detained raises conviction by 16 points — the pressure to plead.

Exercises

Just-identified vs over-identified. Re-estimate Card’s model using nearc2 (near a two-year college) as a second instrument alongside nearc4. Report the 2SLS estimate, the first-stage F, and (in R, summary(..., diagnostics = TRUE); in Python, iv.sargan) the Sargan over-identification test. What does a rejection mean and why is it not a test of the exclusion restriction?

For \(\pi \in \{0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5\}\), run 1,000 replications and record OLS, 2SLS, and the first-stage F. Plot the sampling distribution of 2SLS for each \(\pi\). At what F does 2SLS start to look well-behaved?
Who are the compliers? Using Card, compute the share of compliers implied by the first stage (it is the first-stage coefficient when \(D\) is binary; here educ is continuous, so think of a binary version: educ >= 13). Then compare the mean of black and south among compliers to the full sample using the Abadie (2003) kappa-weighting trick or the simpler ratio-of-first-stages method from the book. Are compliers representative?

title: Session 6 · Instrumental variables
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. With both instruments the estimate rises to ≈ 0.16 (SE ≈ 0.05) and the first-stage F is ≈ 19; the Sargan statistic is 3.6 on 1 df, \(p ≈ 0.06\) — borderline. A rejection would say the two instruments imply different LATEs, which could be heterogeneity rather than invalidity; the test can never validate the exclusion restriction of either instrument on its own.
2. OLS is ≈ 1.8 regardless of \(\pi\) (the endogeneity bias). At \(\pi = 0.05\) the median first-stage F is ≈ 1 and the 2SLS median is ≈ 1.3 with an interquartile range of about 0.8–1.7, pulled toward OLS; at \(\pi = 0.1\) (F ≈ 5) the median is right but the IQR is still 0.6–1.3; by \(\pi = 0.2\) (F ≈ 20) it is tight around 1 (IQR 0.8–1.1). The F ≈ 10 threshold is where the worst behavior fades, not where it ends.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def sim(pi, n=500):
    z = rng.normal(size=n); uv = rng.multivariate_normal([0,0], [[1,.8],[.8,1]], n)
    d = pi*z + uv[:,1]; y = d + uv[:,0]
    df = pd.DataFrame(dict(y=y, d=d, z=z))
    fs = smf.ols("d ~ z", df).fit()
    return smf.ols("y ~ d", df).fit().params["d"], \
           IV2SLS.from_formula("y ~ 1 + [d ~ z]", df).fit().params["d"], fs.fvalue
3. With D = educ >= 13, the first stage on nearc4 is about 0.06, i.e. roughly 6% of the sample are compliers. Using the ratio-of-first-stages method (\(P(x=1 \mid \text{complier}) / P(x=1) = \text{FS}_{x=1} / \text{FS}\)), compliers are far less likely to be Black (ratio ≈ 0.2) and less likely to be Southern (ratio ≈ 0.6) than the full sample. The LATE is for a population that looks quite different from the average respondent — one more reason not to call it “the” return to schooling.

title: Session 4 · Matching and subclassification
text:
Key ideas
Conditional independence (CIA). \((Y^0, Y^1) \perp D \mid X\). Within strata of \(X\), treatment is as good as random. This is the backdoor criterion in potential-outcomes clothing. It is an assumption about unobservables, so no test on the data can confirm it; only the DAG argument can.
Common support. \(0 < P(D=1 \mid X) < 1\). For each covariate profile there must be both treated and untreated units; otherwise you are extrapolating.
Subclassification. Stratify on \(X\), compute the treated-minus-control difference within each stratum, and average using the treated group’s stratum shares (for the ATT). It works beautifully with a few discrete covariates and dies of the curse of dimensionality quickly.
Propensity score. Rosenbaum and Rubin: if CIA holds given \(X\), it also holds given \(p(X) = P(D=1 \mid X)\). One scalar replaces the whole covariate vector. Estimate it with a logit, then stratify on it, weight by it (IPW), or match on it.
Dehejia–Wahba. LaLonde showed that regressions using a non-experimental control group (CPS) badly missed the NSW experimental estimate. Dehejia and Wahba showed that propensity-score methods with a well-specified score and attention to common support get close. The lesson is double-edged: matching can work, and it can fail silently.

title: Session 4 · Matching and subclassification
text:
Walkthrough

Step 1 — Titanic: the simple difference and the subclassified difference
Did first-class passengers survive more because they were first class, or because of who was in first class? Stratify on sex and age.

PythonR


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

t = pd.read_stata("data/titanic.dta")
t["d"]    = (t["class"] == "1st class").astype(int)
t["surv"] = (t["survived"] == "yes").astype(int)
t["man"]  = (t["sex"] == "man").astype(int)
t["adult"]= (t["age"] == "adults").astype(int)

sdo = t.loc[t.d == 1, "surv"].mean() - t.loc[t.d == 0, "surv"].mean()
print("SDO:", round(sdo, 3))

cell = t.groupby(["man", "adult", "d"])["surv"].mean().unstack("d")
diff = cell[1] - cell[0]
w = t[t.d == 1].groupby(["man", "adult"]).size() / (t.d == 1).sum()
print(pd.DataFrame({"diff": diff.round(3), "treated_share": w.round(3)}))
print("Subclassified ATT:", round((diff * w).sum(), 3))


library(tidyverse); library(haven)

t <- read_dta("data/titanic.dta") %>%
  mutate(d = as.integer(class == 1),
         man = as.integer(sex == 1), adult = as.integer(age == 1))
# haven keeps Stata's numeric codes; attributes(t$sex)$labels shows
# 1 = man, and age 1 = adults, class 1 = 1st class, survived 1 = yes

sdo <- with(t, mean(survived[d == 1]) - mean(survived[d == 0]))

att <- t %>%
  group_by(man, adult) %>%
  summarise(diff = mean(survived[d == 1]) - mean(survived[d == 0]),
            n_treated = sum(d == 1), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(w = n_treated / sum(n_treated))
att
sum(att$diff * att$w)




SDO ≈ 0.354: first-class passengers survived 35 points more often. Within sex×age strata the gaps are smaller (adult men: 0.33 vs 0.19; adult women: 0.97 vs 0.63), and the subclassified ATT is ≈ 0.24. A third of the raw gap was who was in first class, not being in first class.



Step 2 — NSW: the experimental benchmark and the naive comparison
nsw_mixtape.dta is the randomized job-training experiment; cps_mixtape.dta is a non-experimental comparison group from the CPS.

PythonR


nsw = pd.read_stata("data/nsw_mixtape.dta")
cps = pd.read_stata("data/cps_mixtape.dta")

exp = nsw.loc[nsw.treat == 1, "re78"].mean() - nsw.loc[nsw.treat == 0, "re78"].mean()
print("experimental effect on 1978 earnings:", round(exp, 0))

d = pd.concat([nsw[nsw.treat == 1], cps[cps.treat == 0]], ignore_index=True)
naive = d.loc[d.treat == 1, "re78"].mean() - d.loc[d.treat == 0, "re78"].mean()
print("NSW treated vs CPS controls:", round(naive, 0))


nsw <- read_dta("data/nsw_mixtape.dta")
cps <- read_dta("data/cps_mixtape.dta")

with(nsw, mean(re78[treat == 1]) - mean(re78[treat == 0]))

d <- bind_rows(filter(nsw, treat == 1), filter(cps, treat == 0))
with(d, mean(re78[treat == 1]) - mean(re78[treat == 0]))




Experimental effect ≈ +$1,794. NSW treated vs CPS controls ≈ −$8,498. The CPS sample is older, better educated and far richer than NSW enrollees; selection bias swamps the effect.



Step 3 — Estimate the propensity score
The Dehejia–Wahba specification: polynomials in age and education, indicators for zero earnings, and an education×earnings interaction.

PythonR


d["age2"] = d.age**2;  d["age3"] = d.age**3;  d["educ2"] = d.educ**2
d["u74"]  = (d.re74 == 0).astype(int);  d["u75"] = (d.re75 == 0).astype(int)
d["interaction1"] = d.educ * d.re74

logit = smf.logit("treat ~ age + age2 + age3 + educ + educ2 + marr + nodegree + black "
                  "+ hisp + re74 + re75 + u74 + u75 + interaction1", data=d).fit(disp=0)
d["pscore"] = logit.predict(d)
print(d.groupby("treat")["pscore"].describe()[["mean", "min", "max"]].round(3))


d <- d %>% mutate(age2 = age^2, age3 = age^3, educ2 = educ^2,
                  u74 = as.integer(re74 == 0), u75 = as.integer(re75 == 0),
                  interaction1 = educ * re74)
logit <- glm(treat ~ age + age2 + age3 + educ + educ2 + marr + nodegree + black +
               hisp + re74 + re75 + u74 + u75 + interaction1,
             family = binomial(), data = d)
d$pscore <- predict(logit, type = "response")
d %>% group_by(treat) %>% summarise(mean = mean(pscore), min = min(pscore), max = max(pscore))

ggplot(d, aes(pscore, fill = factor(treat))) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 50, position = "identity", alpha = 0.5) + theme_minimal()




Mean score ≈ 0.33 for treated and 0.008 for controls. Most CPS people have essentially zero probability of being in NSW. That is the common-support problem in one histogram; the next step trims to the overlap region.



Step 4 — Inverse-probability weighting on the overlap region

PythonR


ov = d[(d.pscore > 0.1) & (d.pscore < 0.9)].copy()
print("units in overlap:", len(ov), " treated:", int(ov.treat.sum()))

# normalized IPW (ATE)
w1 = ov.treat / ov.pscore
w0 = (1 - ov.treat) / (1 - ov.pscore)
y1 = (w1 * ov.re78).sum() / w1.sum()
y0 = (w0 * ov.re78).sum() / w0.sum()
print("normalized IPW estimate:", round(y1 - y0, 0))

# non-normalized version for comparison
print("non-normalized IPW:", round((w1 * ov.re78).mean() - (w0 * ov.re78).mean(), 0))


ov <- d %>% filter(pscore > 0.1, pscore < 0.9) %>%
  mutate(w1 = treat / pscore, w0 = (1 - treat) / (1 - pscore))

y1 <- with(ov, sum(w1 * re78) / sum(w1))
y0 <- with(ov, sum(w0 * re78) / sum(w0))
y1 - y0

with(ov, mean(w1 * re78) - mean(w0 * re78))




About 445 units remain in the overlap region, 147 of them treated. Normalized IPW ≈ +$2,030; non-normalized ≈ +$2,860. Both are within shouting distance of the $1,794 experimental benchmark and nowhere near −$8,498. Normalized weights are more stable; always report them.



Step 5 — Nearest-neighbor matching on the score (ATT)

PythonR


from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

tr = d[d.treat == 1]; co = d[d.treat == 0]
nn = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=1).fit(co[["pscore"]].to_numpy())
_, idx = nn.kneighbors(tr[["pscore"]].to_numpy())
att = (tr.re78.to_numpy() - co.re78.to_numpy()[idx[:, 0]]).mean()
print("1-NN ATT on pscore:", round(att, 0))


library(MatchIt)
m <- matchit(treat ~ age + age2 + age3 + educ + educ2 + marr + nodegree + black +
               hisp + re74 + re75 + u74 + u75 + interaction1,
             data = d, method = "nearest", distance = "glm", replace = TRUE)
md <- match.data(m)
lm(re78 ~ treat, data = md, weights = weights)
summary(m)$sum.matched[, c("Means Treated", "Means Control")]




1-NN ATT ≈ +$1,760, almost exactly the experimental estimate. (MatchIt with replacement gives a similar number; its summary() also shows covariate balance before and after, which is the diagnostic you should always print.)

title: Session 4 · Matching and subclassification
text:
Exercises

Bias reduction by matching. Using training_bias_reduction.dta (8 units, book §5.3), compute the raw SDO, then match each treated unit to the control with the closest X, and compute the ATT. Then compute the bias-corrected matching estimate using a regression of \(Y\) on \(X\) in the control group. Compare all three to each other.
Trimming sensitivity. Rerun Step 4 with overlap windows (0.05, 0.95), (0.1, 0.9) and (0.2, 0.8). How does the estimate and the sample size move? Write two sentences on the bias–variance trade-off involved.
Break CIA. Drop re74 and re75 from the propensity-score model and redo Steps 3–5. What happens, and what does it tell you about which covariates drive selection into NSW?

title: Session 4 · Matching and subclassification
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. Raw SDO = 3.25. Matching each treated unit to the control with the closest X (11→10, 7→8, 5→4, 3→4) gives an ATT of 2.25. The bias-corrected version adjusts each matched pair by \(\hat{\mu}_0(X_{treated}) - \hat{\mu}_0(X_{match})\), where \(\hat{\mu}_0\) is the control-group regression of \(Y\) on \(X\). In this tiny example the \(X\) mismatches are +1, −1, +1, −1, so with a linear \(\hat{\mu}_0\) the corrections cancel and the bias-corrected ATT is also 2.25 — which is itself a useful lesson: the correction matters when mismatches are systematic, not when they are balanced.
tb = pd.read_stata("data/training_bias_reduction.dta")
tr, co = tb[tb.D == 1], tb[tb.D == 0]
mu0 = smf.ols("Y ~ X", co).fit()
rows = []
for _, r in tr.iterrows():
    j = (co.X - r.X).abs().idxmin()
    rows.append((r.Y - co.loc[j, "Y"],
                 r.Y - co.loc[j, "Y"] - (mu0.predict(pd.DataFrame({"X":[r.X]}))[0]
                                        - mu0.predict(pd.DataFrame({"X":[co.loc[j,"X"]]}))[0])))
print(np.mean(rows, axis=0))   # [naive NN ATT, bias-corrected ATT]
2. (0.05, 0.95): ≈ +$1,320 on 601 units; (0.1, 0.9): ≈ +$2,030 on 445; (0.2, 0.8): ≈ +$3,210 on 256. Wider windows keep more controls (lower variance) but include units with poor overlap (more bias); narrower windows do the reverse. The estimate swings by almost $2,000 across reasonable choices — report the sensitivity, not one number.
3. Without lagged earnings the treated group’s mean score drops from 0.33 to about 0.20, and the (0.1, 0.9) IPW estimate flips to ≈ −$2,080. The score no longer captures the dimension that matters most (NSW enrollees had near-zero 1974–75 earnings). Pre-treatment outcomes are the single most important covariate in this design.

title: Session 4 · Matching and subclassification
text:
Facilitator notes






Facilitator notes (click to expand)





The Titanic step is the whole chapter in miniature. Make sure everyone can reproduce the 0.24 by hand (four cells, four weights) before touching propensity scores. The weights are the treated group’s shares, which is what makes it the ATT.
Misconception: the propensity score is a prediction model. You are not trying to predict treatment well; you are trying to achieve covariate balance. A score with AUC 0.99 means no overlap. Say this out loud; it surprises people who come from ML.
Misconception: matching “controls for” unobservables. It does not. The only thing that justifies CIA is the DAG from Session 2.
On the categorical columns. pd.read_stata() returns Stata value labels as categoricals, which is why Step 1 compares to strings. In R, haven keeps the numeric codes with labels attached; attributes(t$class)$labels shows them.
If running short. Drop Step 5; IPW alone makes the point.
Discussion prompts. (a) Why does Dehejia–Wahba work for NSW but Session 2’s discrimination example cannot be fixed by matching? (b) What covariate would you most want that is not in the CPS?
Bridge to next session. Matching needs CIA. RDD gives up on observing everything and instead finds a place where treatment flips for reasons that are locally as good as random.

title: Session 2 · Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Key ideas
A DAG is a set of causal claims, including the arrows you leave out. Nodes are variables; a directed edge \(A \to B\) says \(A\) causes \(B\); the absence of an edge is the strong claim that there is no direct effect. The DAG encodes your prior knowledge of the data-generating process — theory, institutional detail, previous studies — and that is what makes it useful: it forces you to write down what you believe before you touch data.
Paths and what blocks them. A backdoor path from \(D\) to \(Y\) is any path starting with an arrow into \(D\). Backdoor paths carry non-causal association. A path is blocked if it contains a non-collider you condition on, or a collider you do not condition on. A collider is a node where two arrows meet (\(A \to C \leftarrow B\)). Conditioning on a collider (or its descendant) opens the path.
The backdoor criterion. A set of variables \(X\) satisfies the backdoor criterion for \((D, Y)\) if \(X\) blocks every backdoor path and contains no descendant of \(D\). Then conditioning on \(X\) identifies the causal effect of \(D\) on \(Y\). This is the formal version of “conditional independence” and “selection on observables” that Sessions 4 and 7 rely on.
Collider bias is the chapter’s main warning. The book’s discrimination example: female \(\to\) discrimination \(\to\) occupation \(\to\) wage, with discrimination \(\to\) wage directly and unobserved ability \(\to\) occupation and ability \(\to\) wage. Occupation is a collider on the path discrimination \(\to\) occupation \(\leftarrow\) ability \(\to\) wage. “Controlling for occupation,” which sounds like good practice, opens that path and makes discrimination look like it raises wages. The second example — a negative talent–beauty correlation among movie stars when both are independent in the population — is the same mechanism via sample selection.

title: Session 2 · Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Walkthrough

Step 1 — Simulate the discrimination DAG
The DGP, following the book: discrimination is a deterministic function of being female; occupation depends on ability and discrimination; wages depend on discrimination, occupation and ability.

PythonR


import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 10_000
female = rng.binomial(1, 0.5, n)
ability = rng.normal(size=n)
discrimination = female.copy()
occupation = 1 + 2 * ability + 0 * female - 2 * discrimination + rng.normal(size=n)
wage = 1 - 1 * discrimination + 1 * occupation + 2 * ability + rng.normal(size=n)

tb = pd.DataFrame(dict(female=female, ability=ability, discrimination=discrimination,
                       occupation=occupation, wage=wage))


library(tidyverse)
library(estimatr)

set.seed(42)
n <- 10000
tb <- tibble(
  female         = rbinom(n, 1, 0.5),
  ability        = rnorm(n),
  discrimination = female,
  occupation     = 1 + 2 * ability + 0 * female - 2 * discrimination + rnorm(n),
  wage           = 1 - 1 * discrimination + 1 * occupation + 2 * ability + rnorm(n)
)





Step 2 — Three regressions, three answers

PythonR


for f in ["wage ~ female",
          "wage ~ female + occupation",
          "wage ~ female + occupation + ability"]:
    print(f, "\n", smf.ols(f, data=tb).fit().params.round(3), "\n")


lm_1 <- lm(wage ~ female, data = tb)
lm_2 <- lm(wage ~ female + occupation, data = tb)
lm_3 <- lm(wage ~ female + occupation + ability, data = tb)
modelsummary::modelsummary(list("Biased unconditional" = lm_1,
                                "Biased (collider)"    = lm_2,
                                "Unbiased conditional" = lm_3),
                           gof_omit = ".*")




female ≈ −3.0 unconditionally (the total effect: −1 direct, −2 through occupation). Adding occupation flips it to ≈ +0.57 — controlling for a collider makes discrimination look beneficial. Adding ability restores the direct effect ≈ −1.0. Only the third regression could be run in real life if ability were observed, which it usually is not.



Step 3 — Why: trace the paths
Have participants list every path from discrimination to wage and classify each node.








Path
Type
Open when conditioning on occupation?




discrimination → wage
causal (direct)
yes, always


discrimination → occupation → wage
causal (mediated)
blocked (you removed it)


discrimination → occupation ← ability → wage
non-causal, occupation is a collider
opened



Conditioning on occupation removes the mediated effect you probably wanted to keep and opens a spurious path you definitely did not want. Both move the estimate upward.


Step 4 — The talent–beauty collider by selection

PythonR


rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
pop = pd.DataFrame({"beauty": rng.normal(size=10_000),
                    "talent": rng.normal(size=10_000)})
pop["score"] = pop.beauty + pop.talent
cutoff = pop.score.quantile(0.85)
pop["star"] = pop.score >= cutoff

print("population corr:", pop[["beauty", "talent"]].corr().iloc[0, 1].round(3))
print("stars corr:     ", pop.loc[pop.star, ["beauty", "talent"]].corr().iloc[0, 1].round(3))


set.seed(3)
pop <- tibble(beauty = rnorm(10000), talent = rnorm(10000)) %>%
  mutate(score = beauty + talent,
         star  = score >= quantile(score, 0.85))

cor(pop$beauty, pop$talent)
with(filter(pop, star), cor(beauty, talent))

ggplot(pop, aes(beauty, talent, colour = star)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) + theme_minimal()




Population correlation ≈ 0 ; among “stars” it is strongly negative (around −0.65). Nothing causal links beauty and talent; the sample was selected on their sum. Selection on a collider is conditioning on a collider.



Step 5 — (Optional, R only) Let dagitty find the adjustment set
library(dagitty); library(ggdag)

g <- dagitty("dag {
  female -> discrimination
  discrimination -> occupation
  discrimination -> wage
  ability -> occupation
  ability -> wage
  occupation -> wage
}")
adjustmentSets(g, exposure = "discrimination", outcome = "wage", effect = "total")
adjustmentSets(g, exposure = "discrimination", outcome = "wage", effect = "direct")
ggdag(g) + theme_dag()
For the total effect the empty set suffices (no backdoor paths into discrimination). For the direct effect you must condition on occupation and ability. In Python, networkx can draw the graph but has no backdoor solver; this is one place where the R tooling is simply better.

title: Session 2 · Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Exercises

Draw before you regress. A study finds that among hospitalized patients, smoking is negatively associated with COVID-19 severity. Draw a DAG in which smoking does not protect against severe illness but this association appears anyway. Simulate it and show the sign reversal.
Mediator or collider? In the Step 1 DGP, change occupation so that it is caused by female directly (set the 0 * female coefficient to −1) rather than only through discrimination. Re-run the three regressions. Which coefficients change, which do not, and why does the backdoor criterion still give the same answer for the total effect?
Bad controls in the wild. Find one published or newsroom regression (any field) that controls for something plausibly downstream of the treatment. Draw its DAG, and write three sentences on whether the control is a mediator, a collider, or harmless.

title: Session 2 · Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. One DAG: smoking → hospitalization ← severity (both smoking-related illness and severe COVID get you admitted), with smoking having no arrow to severity. Restricting the sample to the hospitalized conditions on the collider.
rng = np.random.default_rng(7); n = 100_000
smoke = rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n)
severity = rng.normal(size=n)                      # independent of smoking
hosp = (0.8*smoke + severity + rng.normal(size=n)) > 1.0
d = pd.DataFrame(dict(smoke=smoke, severity=severity, hosp=hosp))
print(smf.ols("severity ~ smoke", d).fit().params["smoke"])            # ≈ 0
print(smf.ols("severity ~ smoke", d[d.hosp]).fit().params["smoke"])    # < 0
2. The unconditional female coefficient becomes more negative, ≈ −4 (−1 direct via discrimination, −2 via discrimination→occupation, and now −1 more via female→occupation); the collider regression is now ≈ +1.4, even more misleading; the full regression still returns ≈ −1. The collider regression is still wrong, and the full regression now returns the direct effect of female holding occupation fixed, which is −1 (through discrimination). The total effect is still identified with no controls because there are still no arrows into female: randomness of the treatment is what makes the empty adjustment set valid.
3. Open-ended. Common finds: wage regressions that control for occupation or industry; health studies that control for BMI when the treatment affects weight; education studies controlling for test scores measured after the intervention.

title: Session 2 · Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Facilitator notes






Facilitator notes (click to expand)





Make them draw. The biggest failure mode of this session is treating the DAG as decoration for a regression someone already planned. Have each participant sketch the discrimination DAG on paper before Step 2 and predict the sign of the collider regression. Most will predict it stays negative.
Misconception: “more controls are always safer.” Steps 2–3 are the counterexample. Reinforce that the backdoor criterion is a set of variables, and that it can be empty.
Misconception: colliders only matter if you put them in the regression. Step 4 shows selection into the sample does the same thing. Ask: how was this dataset assembled?
If running short. Drop Step 5; it is a nice-to-have for the R users.
Discussion prompts. (a) Where did the arrows in the discrimination DAG come from — data or theory? (b) Can a DAG be tested? (Partially: it implies conditional independencies you can check, but it cannot be derived from data alone.)
Bridge to next session. DAGs tell you what must be true for conditioning to work. Potential outcomes give you the language for what you are estimating — ATE, ATT — and what randomization buys you.

title: Session 1 · Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
Key ideas
Optimization makes everything endogenous. The book’s opening example is price elasticity of demand. Observed prices and quantities are equilibrium outcomes: both supply and demand shifted to produce every point you see, so a regression of quantity on price identifies nothing unless something moved only one curve. Wright’s instrumental-variables solution (Session 6) is the first sighting of the whole book’s agenda: find variation in the cause that is unrelated to everything else that matters.
Regression estimates a conditional expectation function, not a causal effect. Chapter 2 builds up to three theorems. The linear CEF theorem says if the CEF is linear, regression recovers it. The best linear predictor theorem says regression is always the best linear approximation to the CEF, whether or not it is linear. The regression CEF theorem says regression also gives the best linear approximation to the CEF itself. None of these say anything about causation; they say what the numbers mean descriptively. Causal content enters only through assumptions about the error term (mean independence, \(E[u \mid x] = 0\)), and those assumptions are what the rest of the book is about.
Regression anatomy. The coefficient on \(x_1\) in a multiple regression equals the bivariate regression of \(y\) on the residual from regressing \(x_1\) on the other covariates: \[\beta_1 = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(y, \tilde{x}_1)}{\mathrm{Var}(\tilde{x}_1)}, \qquad \tilde{x}_1 = x_1 - \hat{E}[x_1 \mid x_2, \dots, x_k].\] This is the Frisch–Waugh–Lovell theorem, and it is the single most useful mechanical fact about regression: “controlling for” means “using only the part of \(x_1\) that the controls cannot predict.”
Standard errors. Conventional OLS standard errors assume homoskedasticity. Heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1, Stata’s robust) standard errors do not. When observations share a shock (students in the same classroom, firms in the same state), errors are correlated within groups and you need cluster-robust standard errors; the robust-versus-conventional gap on a single regression is a diagnostic, not a decision rule.

title: Session 1 · Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
Walkthrough

Step 1 — Load auto and run a bivariate regression

PythonR


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

auto = pd.read_stata("data/auto.dta")
auto.head()

m1 = smf.ols("price ~ length", data=auto).fit()
print(m1.summary().tables[1])


library(tidyverse)
library(haven)
library(estimatr)

auto <- read_dta("data/auto.dta")
glimpse(auto)

m1 <- lm(price ~ length, data = auto)
summary(m1)




Intercept ≈ −4585, slope on length ≈ 57.2 dollars per inch. Ask the room: is a longer car caused to be more expensive? What else do longer cars have more of?



Step 2 — Add controls and watch the sign flip

PythonR


m2 = smf.ols("price ~ length + weight + headroom + mpg", data=auto).fit()
print(m2.params.round(2))


m2 <- lm(price ~ length + weight + headroom + mpg, data = auto)
coef(m2)




length ≈ −94.5, weight ≈ 4.34, headroom ≈ −491, mpg ≈ −88. Conditional on weight, headroom and fuel economy, a longer car is cheaper. Neither coefficient is “the” effect of length; they answer different descriptive questions.



Step 3 — Reproduce the length coefficient with regression anatomy
Regress length on the other covariates, keep the residual, and regress price on that residual alone.

PythonR


aux = smf.ols("length ~ weight + headroom + mpg", data=auto).fit()
auto["length_resid"] = aux.resid

m3 = smf.ols("price ~ length_resid", data=auto).fit()
print(m3.params.round(2))

# the formula directly
cov = np.cov(auto["price"], auto["length_resid"], ddof=1)[0, 1]
var = auto["length_resid"].var(ddof=1)
print(cov / var)


auto <- auto %>%
  mutate(length_resid = resid(lm(length ~ weight + headroom + mpg, data = auto)))

m3 <- lm(price ~ length_resid, data = auto)
coef(m3)

cov(auto$price, auto$length_resid) / var(auto$length_resid)




The slope on length_resid is −94.5, identical to the multiple-regression coefficient. The intercept differs (it is just the mean of price, ≈ 6165) because the residual has mean zero.



Step 4 — Robust versus conventional standard errors
Simulate data whose error variance grows with \(|x|\), so homoskedasticity fails.

PythonR


rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n = 10_000
x = rng.normal(size=n)
u = rng.normal(size=n) * (1 + np.abs(x))      # heteroskedastic
y = 5.5 * x + 12 * u
sim = pd.DataFrame({"x": x, "y": y})

conv = smf.ols("y ~ x", data=sim).fit()
rob  = smf.ols("y ~ x", data=sim).fit(cov_type="HC1")
print("conventional SE:", round(conv.bse["x"], 3))
print("HC1 robust SE:  ", round(rob.bse["x"], 3))


set.seed(1)
n <- 10000
x <- rnorm(n)
u <- rnorm(n) * (1 + abs(x))
y <- 5.5 * x + 12 * u
sim <- tibble(x, y)

conv <- lm(y ~ x, data = sim)
rob  <- lm_robust(y ~ x, data = sim, se_type = "HC1")
sqrt(diag(vcov(conv)))["x"]
rob$std.error["x"]




Conventional SE ≈ 0.22, robust SE ≈ 0.31 (your exact numbers depend on the seed). The point estimate is unchanged; only the uncertainty was wrong. Discuss: in which direction does heteroskedasticity bias the conventional SE here, and why?



Step 5 — Clustered standard errors
Now give the data a group structure with a shared group-level shock.

PythonR


g = rng.integers(0, 50, size=n)                   # 50 clusters
group_shock = rng.normal(size=50)[g]
x = rng.normal(size=n) + group_shock
y = 2 * x + 5 * group_shock + rng.normal(size=n)
cl = pd.DataFrame({"x": x, "y": y, "g": g})

plain   = smf.ols("y ~ x", data=cl).fit(cov_type="HC1")
cluster = smf.ols("y ~ x", data=cl).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": cl["g"]})
print(plain.bse["x"].round(3), cluster.bse["x"].round(3))


g <- sample(0:49, n, replace = TRUE)
group_shock <- rnorm(50)[g + 1]
x <- rnorm(n) + group_shock
y <- 2 * x + 5 * group_shock + rnorm(n)
cl <- tibble(x, y, g)

lm_robust(y ~ x, data = cl, se_type = "HC1")$std.error["x"]
lm_robust(y ~ x, data = cl, clusters = g)$std.error["x"]




The clustered SE is several times the robust SE. The group shock is in both \(x\) and the error, so the point estimate is also biased upward from 2 — a preview of the omitted-variable problem the rest of the book attacks. Clustering fixes inference, never identification.

Explain in two sentences what conditioning on the host’s informed choice does.

title: Session 1 · Why causal inference, and regression as a tool
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. For mpg: residualize mpg on length + weight + headroom, regress price on the residual; slope is −87.96. For weight: residualize on length + headroom + mpg; slope is 4.34. Compare each residual’s variance to the variable’s raw variance: mpg keeps about 34% of its variation after partialling out the others, while length and weight each keep only about 10% (they are nearly collinear with one another). Precision is \(\sigma^2 / (n \cdot \mathrm{Var}(\tilde{x}_k))\) scaled by the variable’s units, so the coefficient whose regressor retains the most of its own variation — mpg — is the one estimated most precisely relative to its scale; length and weight are fighting over the same variation.
2. Stay wins ≈ 1/3, switch wins ≈ 2/3. With a random host (void if the car is revealed), both strategies win 1/2 of the non-void games. The informed host’s choice is a function of where the car is, so conditioning on it moves probability; the random host’s choice is independent of the car’s location, so it carries no information.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); N = 100_000
car = rng.integers(0, 3, N); pick = rng.integers(0, 3, N)
# informed host opens a goat door that is not the pick
host = np.array([next(d for d in rng.permutation(3) if d != c and d != p) for c, p in zip(car, pick)])
switch = 3 - pick - host
print((pick == car).mean(), (switch == car).mean())
3. Homoskedastic case: the two SEs agree to two decimals. At n = 50 the robust SE has a noticeably larger spread across replications (it estimates more parameters from the same data). Researchers accept the variability because the robust estimator is consistent under a wider set of DGPs, but with tiny samples HC2/HC3 corrections are advisable.

title: Session 3 · Potential outcomes
text:
Key ideas
Potential outcomes. Each unit \(i\) has \(Y_i^1\) (outcome if treated) and \(Y_i^0\) (if not). The individual treatment effect is \(\delta_i = Y_i^1 - Y_i^0\). We observe only \(Y_i = D_i Y_i^1 + (1 - D_i) Y_i^0\) — the switching equation. The missing potential outcome is the fundamental problem of causal inference; every design in this book is a strategy for filling it in credibly.
Estimands. \(ATE = E[\delta]\); \(ATT = E[\delta \mid D = 1]\); \(ATU = E[\delta \mid D = 0]\). They differ whenever effects are heterogeneous and treatment is selected on them.
The decomposition. The simple difference in outcomes (SDO) is \[E[Y \mid D=1] - E[Y \mid D=0] = ATE + \underbrace{E[Y^0 \mid D=1] - E[Y^0 \mid D=0]}_{\text{selection bias}} + \underbrace{(1-\pi)(ATT - ATU)}_{\text{HTE bias}}.\] Selection bias: treated units would have done differently even untreated. HTE bias: treated units gain differently from treatment. Randomization makes \(D\) independent of \((Y^0, Y^1)\), so both bias terms are zero and the SDO is the ATE.
Randomization inference. Fisher’s sharp null, \(H_0: \delta_i = 0\) for every \(i\), fills in every missing potential outcome (they equal the observed ones). Under it, you can recompute the test statistic for every possible assignment and get an exact \(p\)-value with no distributional assumptions and no appeal to large samples. It is the right tool for small experiments and a useful stress test for any design.

title: Session 3 · Potential outcomes
text:
Walkthrough

Step 1 — Yule (1899): regression without a design
Yule regressed changes in pauperism on changes in out-relief (welfare outside the poorhouse), with controls for the share of elderly and population growth, and concluded out-relief caused pauperism.

PythonR


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf

yule = pd.read_stata("data/yule.dta")
print(smf.ols("paup ~ outrelief + old + pop", data=yule).fit().summary().tables[1])


library(tidyverse); library(haven); library(estimatr)

yule <- read_dta("data/yule.dta")
lm(paup ~ outrelief + old + pop, data = yule) %>% summary()




outrelief ≈ 0.75: a 10% rise in out-relief is associated with a 7.5% rise in pauperism. Ask: what is the obvious reverse-causation story, and what would a DAG for this look like? (Hint: local poverty shocks drive both.)



Step 2 — Thornton (2008): a real experiment
Thornton randomized cash incentives for learning one’s HIV status in rural Malawi. any is the randomized incentive indicator; got is whether the person collected their result.

PythonR


hiv = pd.read_stata("data/thornton_hiv.dta").dropna(subset=["got", "any"])
print(hiv.groupby("any")["got"].mean().round(3))

m = smf.ols("got ~ any", data=hiv).fit(cov_type="cluster",
                                        cov_kwds={"groups": hiv["villnum"]})
print(m.summary().tables[1])


hiv <- read_dta("data/thornton_hiv.dta") %>% drop_na(got, any)
hiv %>% group_by(any) %>% summarise(got = mean(got), n = n())

lm_robust(got ~ any, data = hiv, clusters = villnum)




34% of the no-incentive group learned their status; 79% of the incentive group did. The difference, 0.45 (SE ≈ 0.02 clustered by village), is the ATE because any was randomized. Note how little work the regression is doing; the design did it.



Step 3 — Fisher’s exact \(p\)-value on the 8-unit toy data
ri.dta has four treated and four control units. The sharp null says every unit’s \(Y^1 = Y^0 = Y\), so we can recompute the difference in means for all \(\binom{8}{4} = 70\) assignments.

PythonR


import itertools

ri = pd.read_stata("data/ri.dta")
y = ri["y"].to_numpy()
d = ri["d"].to_numpy()
obs = y[d == 1].mean() - y[d == 0].mean()

stats = []
for treated in itertools.combinations(range(8), 4):
    mask = np.zeros(8, dtype=bool); mask[list(treated)] = True
    stats.append(y[mask].mean() - y[~mask].mean())
stats = np.array(stats)

p = (np.abs(stats) >= abs(obs)).mean()
print(f"observed diff = {obs:.2f}, exact two-sided p = {p:.3f} over {len(stats)} assignments")


ri <- read_dta("data/ri.dta")
y <- ri$y; d <- ri$d
obs <- mean(y[d == 1]) - mean(y[d == 0])

combos <- combn(8, 4)
stats <- apply(combos, 2, function(idx) mean(y[idx]) - mean(y[-idx]))
p <- mean(abs(stats) >= abs(obs))
c(observed = obs, p_value = p, n_assignments = ncol(combos))




Observed difference = 1.0; 60 of 70 assignments give a difference at least that large in absolute value, so \(p ≈\) 0.86. With eight units you learn almost nothing, and the exact test says so without pretending otherwise.



Step 4 — Randomization inference on Thornton
With 4,820 people there are too many assignments to enumerate; sample 1,000 random permutations of the treatment vector.

PythonR


rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
got = hiv["got"].to_numpy(); anyv = hiv["any"].to_numpy()
obs = got[anyv == 1].mean() - got[anyv == 0].mean()

perm = np.empty(1000)
for i in range(1000):
    a = rng.permutation(anyv)
    perm[i] = got[a == 1].mean() - got[a == 0].mean()

print("observed:", round(obs, 3))
print("largest |placebo| diff:", np.abs(perm).max().round(3))
print("p-value:", (np.abs(perm) >= abs(obs)).mean())


set.seed(1)
obs <- with(hiv, mean(got[any == 1]) - mean(got[any == 0]))
perm <- replicate(1000, {
  a <- sample(hiv$any)
  mean(hiv$got[a == 1]) - mean(hiv$got[a == 0])
})
c(observed = obs, max_placebo = max(abs(perm)), p = mean(abs(perm) >= abs(obs)))

ggplot(tibble(perm), aes(perm)) + geom_histogram(bins = 40) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs, colour = "red") + theme_minimal()




The largest placebo difference is around 0.07; the observed 0.45 is more than six times further out. $p = $ 0 at 1,000 draws. The histogram with the red line is the slide to keep: it is the sampling distribution under the sharp null.

Exercises

Decompose the bias. Build a population of 10,000 units with \(Y^0 \sim N(10, 2)\) and \(\delta_i \sim N(2, 1)\). Let units select into treatment when \(Y^1 - Y^0 > 2.3\) (they take it if it helps them more than average). Compute the true ATE, ATT, ATU, the SDO, and verify the decomposition formula numerically term by term.
RI with a different statistic. Redo Step 3 using the difference in medians and then the Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistic. Do the \(p\)-values change? When would you want a statistic other than the mean difference?
Thornton heterogeneity. The incentive amount tinc varied. Plot the share who got results by incentive amount (bin it) and test whether any positive incentive versus none explains most of the effect. What does this say about the ATE being an average over very different \(\delta_i\)?

title: Session 3 · Potential outcomes
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1.
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); N = 10_000
y0 = rng.normal(10, 2, N); delta = rng.normal(2, 1, N); y1 = y0 + delta
D = (delta > 2.3).astype(int); Y = np.where(D == 1, y1, y0)
ATE = delta.mean(); ATT = delta[D==1].mean(); ATU = delta[D==0].mean()
SDO = Y[D==1].mean() - Y[D==0].mean()
sel = y0[D==1].mean() - y0[D==0].mean()
pi = D.mean()
print(SDO, ATE + sel + (1-pi)*(ATT-ATU))
Selection bias is ≈ 0 here (selection is on \(\delta\), not on \(Y^0\)), but HTE bias is large: ATT ≈ 3.0 vs ATU ≈ 1.4, so the SDO (≈ 3.0) overstates the ATE (= 2.0) by about 1.
2. The median-difference \(p\)-value on 8 units is similar (≈ 0.9). KS is more sensitive to distributional differences beyond location; use it when treatment might change spread or shape rather than the mean.
3. Collection rates jump from 34% at zero incentive to about 67% for the smallest positive amounts (under half a dollar), then rise to about 85% for amounts over a dollar. Most of the 0.45 ATE is the extensive margin; individual \(\delta_i\) clearly differ (for people who would have collected anyway, \(\delta_i = 0\)).

title: Session 5 · Regression discontinuity
text:
Key ideas
The design. Treatment \(D\) is a deterministic function of a running variable \(X\) relative to a cutoff \(c_0\): \(D = 1[X \geq c_0]\) (sharp) or jumps in probability there (fuzzy). Units just above and just below the cutoff differ in treatment but, if nothing else jumps at \(c_0\), in nothing else.
Identification by continuity. \(E[Y^0 \mid X]\) and \(E[Y^1 \mid X]\) must be continuous at \(c_0\). Then \[\delta_{SRD} = \lim_{x \downarrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x] - \lim_{x \uparrow c_0} E[Y \mid X = x].\] No conditional-independence assumption, no need to observe confounders: everything that matters is a smooth function of \(X\) except the treatment.
Estimation is a bias–variance problem. You need the two limits. Global polynomials use all the data but let far-away observations drive the fit at the cutoff (Gelman and Imbens’s warning against high-order polynomials). Local linear regression within a bandwidth \(h\) is the modern default, with rdrobust choosing \(h\) and correcting for bias. The honest report shows several.
Threats and checks. If units can precisely manipulate \(X\) (sorting just above a test-score cutoff), continuity fails. Check that the density of \(X\) is smooth at \(c_0\) (McCrary) and that pre-determined covariates do not jump there. Fuzzy RD is IV with the cutoff as instrument, which is next session’s topic.
The LMB question. Do close elections reveal whether politicians converge to the median voter (Downs) or diverge to their party’s preferences? In a 50–50 district the party barely won is as-good-as random; if the winner’s voting score jumps at the 50% line, parties do not converge.

title: Session 5 · Regression discontinuity
text:
Walkthrough

Step 1 — Look at the data

PythonR


import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

lmb = (pd.read_stata("data/close_elections_lmb.dta")
         .dropna(subset=["score", "lagdemvoteshare", "lagdemocrat"]))   # 11 rows lack a lagged vote share
lmb["dem_c"] = lmb.lagdemvoteshare - 0.5          # centered running variable

bins = lmb.groupby(pd.cut(lmb.lagdemvoteshare, np.arange(0, 1.01, 0.02)), observed=True)["score"].mean()
ax = bins.plot(marker="o", linestyle="")
ax.axvline(x=24.5, color="grey")                   # the 0.50 bin boundary
ax.set_xlabel("Democratic vote share, previous election (binned)")
ax.set_ylabel("ADA score of the representative")
plt.show()


library(tidyverse); library(haven); library(estimatr)

lmb <- read_dta("data/close_elections_lmb.dta") %>%
  drop_na(score, lagdemvoteshare, lagdemocrat) %>%
  mutate(dem_c = lagdemvoteshare - 0.5)

lmb %>%
  mutate(bin = cut(lagdemvoteshare, seq(0, 1, 0.02))) %>%
  group_by(bin) %>% summarise(score = mean(score), x = mean(lagdemvoteshare)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, score)) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = 0.5) + theme_minimal()




A cloud of points rising with Democratic vote share, with a visible vertical jump at 0.5 of roughly 20–40 ADA points. score is the ADA liberalism score of the sitting representative; lagdemocrat is whether a Democrat won the previous election, which is the treatment.



Step 2 — The naive and the close-election comparisons

PythonR


def fit(df, formula):
    return smf.ols(formula, data=df).fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": df["id"]})

all_ = fit(lmb, "score ~ lagdemocrat")
close = fit(lmb[(lmb.lagdemvoteshare > 0.48) & (lmb.lagdemvoteshare < 0.52)], "score ~ lagdemocrat")
print("all elections:  ", all_.params["lagdemocrat"].round(2), all_.bse["lagdemocrat"].round(2))
print("within ±2 points:", close.params["lagdemocrat"].round(2), close.bse["lagdemocrat"].round(2),
      " n =", int(close.nobs))


lm_robust(score ~ lagdemocrat, data = lmb, clusters = id)
lm_robust(score ~ lagdemocrat,
          data = filter(lmb, lagdemvoteshare > 0.48, lagdemvoteshare < 0.52),
          clusters = id)




All elections: ≈ 31.5. Within ±2 points of the cutoff: ≈ 21.3 (SE ≈ 2, n = 915). The simple comparison is contaminated by district ideology; the close-election estimate is the book’s headline number.



Step 3 — Polynomial specifications, global and local
Interact the treatment with the centered running variable so each side gets its own slope.

PythonR


lmb["dem_c2"] = lmb.dem_c**2
local = lmb[(lmb.lagdemvoteshare > 0.45) & (lmb.lagdemvoteshare < 0.55)]

specs = {
  "linear, all data":     fit(lmb,   "score ~ lagdemocrat * dem_c"),
  "linear, ±5 points":    fit(local, "score ~ lagdemocrat * dem_c"),
  "quadratic, all data":  fit(lmb,   "score ~ lagdemocrat * (dem_c + dem_c2)"),
  "quadratic, ±5 points": fit(local, "score ~ lagdemocrat * (dem_c + dem_c2)"),
}
for k, m in specs.items():
    print(f"{k:22s} {m.params['lagdemocrat']:6.2f}  (SE {m.bse['lagdemocrat']:.2f})")


local <- filter(lmb, lagdemvoteshare > 0.45, lagdemvoteshare < 0.55)
lmb   <- mutate(lmb, dem_c2 = dem_c^2); local <- mutate(local, dem_c2 = dem_c^2)

list(
  "linear, all"     = lm_robust(score ~ lagdemocrat * dem_c, data = lmb,   clusters = id),
  "linear, ±5"      = lm_robust(score ~ lagdemocrat * dem_c, data = local, clusters = id),

  "quadratic, ±5"   = lm_robust(score ~ lagdemocrat * (dem_c + dem_c2), data = local, clusters = id)
) %>% map_dbl(~ coef(.x)["lagdemocrat"])




Linear/all ≈ 37.7; linear/±5 ≈ 19.8; quadratic/all ≈ 18.1; quadratic/±5 ≈ 25.6. The sign and rough size are robust; the exact number is not. Show the room all four and ask which they would put in the abstract. The honest answer is “the local ones, with the bandwidth stated.”

for c in [0.40, 0.45, 0.55, 0.60]:
    sub = lmb[(lmb.lagdemvoteshare > c - 0.05) & (lmb.lagdemvoteshare < c + 0.05)].copy()

3. lagdemocrat predicts democrat with a jump of ≈ 0.42 at the cutoff — winning narrowly last time makes you much more likely to hold the seat (incumbency). The score question is sharp because treatment is defined as who won last time. It would be fuzzy if the treatment of interest were “a Democrat holds the seat now,” since that only jumps partially at the cutoff; then $= $ (jump in score) / (jump in Democrat), which is an IV estimate.
