title: Session 7 · Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
Key ideas
The fixed-effects model. \(Y_{it} = \delta D_{it} + \mathbf{X}_{it}\beta + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}\). The unit effect \(u_i\) can be correlated with \(D_{it}\) in any way; FE removes it by comparing each unit to itself across time. Three equivalent implementations: unit dummies, demeaning every variable within unit, or first-differencing (with two periods).
What FE needs. Strict exogeneity: \(E[\varepsilon_{it} \mid D_{i1}, \dots, D_{iT}, u_i] = 0\). Time-varying unobservables that move with \(D\) are still a problem. Reverse causality and feedback (today’s shock affects tomorrow’s treatment) violate it. FE also needs within variation; a regressor that never changes for a unit is absorbed.
The SASP question. Sex workers charge more for unprotected sex. Is that a compensating differential for risk, or do higher-priced providers simply differ in ways that also make them more likely to offer it? The panel follows the same provider across clients, so provider-level unobservables drop out.
The 2×2 DiD. Two groups, two periods. \(\hat{\delta} = (\bar{Y}_{T,post} - \bar{Y}_{T,pre}) - (\bar{Y}_{C,post} - \bar{Y}_{C,pre})\). The identifying assumption is parallel trends: absent treatment, the treated group’s outcome would have moved by the same amount as the control group’s. It is a statement about a counterfactual and is untestable in the 2×2 case. As a regression: \(Y = \alpha + \beta\,\text{Treat} + \gamma\,\text{Post} + \delta\,(\text{Treat} \times \text{Post}) + e\).
John Snow. In 1854 London, the Lambeth water company had moved its intake upstream of the sewage; Southwark & Vauxhall had not. Cholera deaths fell in Lambeth-served households and rose elsewhere. It is the first DiD and still one of the cleanest.

Step 1 — SASP: pooled OLS

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from linearmodels.panel import PanelOLS

sasp = pd.read_stata("data/sasp_panel.dta", convert_categoricals=False)

timevar = ["unsafe", "llength", "reg", "asq_cl", "appearance_cl", "provider_second",
           "asian_cl", "black_cl", "hispanic_cl", "othrace_cl", "hot", "massage_cl", "age_cl"]
fixed   = ["age", "asq", "bmi", "hispanic", "black", "other", "asian", "schooling",
           "cohab", "married", "divorced", "separated"]
sasp = sasp.dropna(subset=["lnw", "id"] + timevar + fixed)

pooled = smf.ols("lnw ~ " + " + ".join(timevar + fixed), data=sasp)\
            .fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": sasp["id"]})
print("pooled OLS, unsafe:", pooled.params["unsafe"].round(3), " SE", pooled.bse["unsafe"].round(3))


library(tidyverse); library(haven); library(fixest)

sasp <- read_dta("data/sasp_panel.dta")
timevar <- c("unsafe","llength","reg","asq_cl","appearance_cl","provider_second",
             "asian_cl","black_cl","hispanic_cl","othrace_cl","hot","massage_cl","age_cl")
fixed   <- c("age","asq","bmi","hispanic","black","other","asian","schooling",
             "cohab","married","divorced","separated")

f_pooled <- as.formula(paste("lnw ~", paste(c(timevar, fixed), collapse = " + ")))
pooled <- feols(f_pooled, data = sasp, cluster = ~id)
coeftable(pooled)["unsafe", ]




unsafe ≈ 0.00 (SE 0.03): pooled across providers, there is no price premium for unprotected sex once client and provider characteristics are controlled. About 1,500 sessions enter after dropping missing values.



Step 2 — Fixed effects, three ways

PythonR


# (a) demeaning by hand
dm = sasp.copy()
for v in ["lnw"] + timevar:
    dm[v] = sasp[v] - sasp.groupby("id")[v].transform("mean")
fe_dm = smf.ols("lnw ~ " + " + ".join(timevar), data=dm)\
           .fit(cov_type="cluster", cov_kwds={"groups": dm["id"]})

# (b) unit dummies (slow with many ids, but transparent)
fe_dummy = smf.ols("lnw ~ " + " + ".join(timevar) + " + C(id)", data=sasp).fit()

# (c) PanelOLS
p = sasp.set_index(["id", "session"])
fe_panel = PanelOLS.from_formula("lnw ~ " + " + ".join(timevar) + " + EntityEffects", data=p)\
             .fit(cov_type="clustered", cluster_entity=True)

print("demeaned:", fe_dm.params["unsafe"].round(3),
      " dummies:", fe_dummy.params["unsafe"].round(3),
      " PanelOLS:", fe_panel.params["unsafe"].round(3), " SE", fe_panel.std_errors["unsafe"].round(3))


f_fe <- as.formula(paste("lnw ~", paste(timevar, collapse = " + "), "| id"))
fe <- feols(f_fe, data = sasp, cluster = ~id)
coeftable(fe)["unsafe", ]

# the same thing by hand
dm <- sasp %>% group_by(id) %>%
  mutate(across(all_of(c("lnw", timevar)), ~ .x - mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE))) %>% ungroup()
coef(lm(as.formula(paste("lnw ~", paste(timevar, collapse = " + "))), data = dm))["unsafe"]

etable(pooled, fe, keep = "unsafe")




All three give unsafe ≈ 0.05 (SE ≈ 0.024): within the same provider, an unprotected session commands about a 5% premium. The time-invariant provider characteristics (age, schooling, race, marital status) are absorbed; try adding them to the FE model and watch them vanish or error. The dummy version’s SE is wrong (not clustered) — note it and move on.



Step 3 — Why they differ
The pooled estimate mixes two comparisons: within a provider (does she charge more when the session is unprotected?) and between providers (do the ones who offer unprotected sex charge more in general?). FE keeps only the first. The near-zero pooled estimate means the between-provider correlation is negative enough to cancel the within premium: providers willing to offer unprotected sex are, on average, lower-priced. That is exactly the selection story FE was built to remove.


Step 4 — John Snow’s cholera DiD by hand
Deaths per 10,000 households, from the book’s Table 9.1:




1849 (pre)
1854 (post)




Southwark & Vauxhall (control)
135
147


Lambeth (treated: moved intake upstream in 1852)
85
19




PythonR


snow = pd.DataFrame({
    "company": ["SV", "SV", "Lambeth", "Lambeth"],
    "year":    [1849, 1854, 1849, 1854],
    "deaths":  [135, 147, 85, 19],
})
snow["treat"] = (snow.company == "Lambeth").astype(int)
snow["post"]  = (snow.year == 1854).astype(int)

by_hand = (19 - 85) - (147 - 135)
reg = smf.ols("deaths ~ treat * post", data=snow).fit()
print("by hand:", by_hand, "  regression:", reg.params["treat:post"].round(1))


snow <- tibble(company = c("SV","SV","Lambeth","Lambeth"),
               year = c(1849, 1854, 1849, 1854),
               deaths = c(135, 147, 85, 19)) %>%
  mutate(treat = as.integer(company == "Lambeth"), post = as.integer(year == 1854))

(19 - 85) - (147 - 135)
coef(lm(deaths ~ treat * post, data = snow))["treat:post"]




Both give −78 deaths per 10,000 households. With four cells there are no standard errors — the regression is exactly identified — which is the point: the 2×2 is an identification argument, and inference needs more groups or more periods (next session).



Step 5 — Draw the counterfactual
Sketch (or plot) the four points. The DiD estimate is the gap between Lambeth’s actual 1854 value (19) and what parallel trends says it would have been: \(85 + (147 - 135) = 97\). Ask the room what would make the dotted line wrong — for example, if Lambeth’s neighborhoods were already becoming cleaner for other reasons.

Exercises

First differences vs FE. Keep only providers with exactly two sessions in the SASP data (about 68 of them). Estimate the unsafe effect by first-differencing (session 2 minus session 1, regression without a constant) and by FE on the demeaned data. Show they are identical with \(T = 2\), explain what adding a constant to the FD regression corresponds to in the FE model, and say in one sentence why FD and FE diverge for \(T > 2\).
What FE cannot fix. Simulate a panel of 500 units × 5 periods where \(D_{it}\) responds to last period’s shock: \(D_{it} = 1[\varepsilon_{i,t-1} > 0]\). Set the true effect to 1. Show that FE is biased and explain which assumption failed.
Snow with a placebo. Suppose a third company, “Chelsea,” had deaths of 110 in 1849 and 125 in 1854 and did not move its intake. Compute the DiD of Chelsea vs Southwark & Vauxhall. What does a near-zero number tell you about parallel trends, and what does it not tell you?

title: Session 7 · Panel data and the 2×2 difference-in-differences
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. With \(T = 2\), demeaning and differencing use the same single within-unit contrast, so the estimates coincide exactly (≈ −0.06 in this small subsample — note it has the opposite sign from the full-panel FE estimate, a reminder that 68 providers is not much data). Adding a constant to the FD regression is the same as adding a period fixed effect to the FE model. For \(T > 2\) FE uses all pairwise contrasts weighted by the within-unit variance, while FD uses only adjacent-period contrasts; they differ, and FD is more robust when \(\varepsilon_{it}\) is a random walk.
2. FE is biased because strict exogeneity fails: \(D_{it}\) depends on \(\varepsilon_{i,t-1}\), and demeaning puts every period’s \(\varepsilon\) into every period’s transformed error. The bias shrinks as \(T\) grows (it is of order \(1/T\)). First differencing also fails here, because \(\Delta D_{it}\) depends on \(\varepsilon_{i,t-1}\) which is in \(\Delta \varepsilon_{it}\).
rng = np.random.default_rng(0); N, T = 500, 5
e = rng.normal(size=(N, T)); D = np.zeros((N, T), int); D[:, 1:] = (e[:, :-1] > 0)
u = rng.normal(size=(N, 1)); Y = 1 * D + u + e
df = pd.DataFrame({"y": Y.ravel(), "d": D.ravel(), "i": np.repeat(np.arange(N), T), "t": np.tile(np.arange(T), N)})
dm = df.assign(y=df.y - df.groupby("i").y.transform("mean"), d=df.d - df.groupby("i").d.transform("mean"))
print(smf.ols("y ~ d", dm).fit().params["d"])    # noticeably below 1
3. Chelsea vs S&V: \((125 - 110) - (147 - 135) = 3\): two untreated companies moved in parallel. That is evidence consistent with parallel trends for the untreated, which makes the assumption more plausible for Lambeth. It does not test Lambeth’s own counterfactual trend, which is unobservable by construction.

title: Session 9 · Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
Key ideas
The comparative case study. One treated aggregate unit (a state, a country), a handful of candidate controls, and a long pre-period. DiD with one treated unit has no credible standard error and picks the control arbitrarily. Synthetic control replaces the choice with an algorithm: find weights \(w_j \geq 0\), \(\sum w_j = 1\), over donor units \(j\) that make the weighted average of donors match the treated unit’s pre-treatment outcomes and predictors as closely as possible. The post-period gap between the treated unit and its synthetic version is the estimated effect.
Why the constraints matter. Non-negativity and summing to one keep the synthetic unit inside the convex hull of the donors: no extrapolation, and the weights are interpretable (“Texas is 45% California, 32% Ohio…”). A poor pre-period fit means the method has nothing to say; report the pre-period RMSPE.
Inference by placebo. Reassign treatment to each donor in turn, fit its synthetic control, and compute its post/pre RMSPE ratio. If the treated unit’s ratio is extreme relative to the placebo distribution, the effect is unlikely to be luck. The “p-value” is the treated unit’s rank divided by the number of units.
The Texas question. Texas massively expanded prison capacity in 1993–1994. Black male incarceration roughly doubled over the following years. Did the building cause the filling, relative to a synthetic Texas built from other states?
What the book wants you to leave with. Every chapter answered the same question: where does the exogenous variation come from? Randomization (Ch. 4), observable selection you can model (Ch. 5), a threshold (Ch. 6), an instrument (Ch. 7), within-unit change (Ch. 8), a policy difference across groups and time (Ch. 9), a weighted comparison unit (Ch. 10). The method follows the source of variation, never the reverse.

Step 1 — Fit the synthetic Texas
Predictors follow the book: poverty and income averaged over the pre-period, plus the Black male prison population in selected years, alcohol consumption, AIDS incidence, the Black population share and the 15–19 share.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from pysyncon import Dataprep, Synth        # pip install pysyncon

tx = pd.read_stata("data/texas.dta", convert_categoricals=False)
names = tx.drop_duplicates("statefip").set_index("statefip")["state"]
TEXAS = 48
donors = [s for s in tx.statefip.unique() if s != TEXAS]

dp = Dataprep(
    foo=tx, dependent="bmprison", unit_variable="statefip", time_variable="year",
    treatment_identifier=TEXAS, controls_identifier=donors,
    predictors=["poverty", "income"], predictors_op="mean", time_predictors_prior=range(1985, 1994),
    special_predictors=[
        ("bmprison", range(1988, 1989), "mean"), ("bmprison", range(1990, 1991), "mean"),
        ("bmprison", range(1991, 1992), "mean"), ("bmprison", range(1992, 1993), "mean"),
        ("alcohol", range(1990, 1991), "mean"),  ("aidscapita", range(1990, 1992), "mean"),
        ("black", range(1990, 1992), "mean"),    ("perc1519", range(1990, 1991), "mean"),
    ],
    time_optimize_ssr=range(1985, 1994),
)
synth = Synth()
synth.fit(dataprep=dp, optim_method="BFGS", optim_initial="ols")   # ~20 s; the default Nelder-Mead can take many minutes
w = synth.weights(); w.index = [names[i] for i in w.index]
print(w[w > 0.01].round(3))


library(tidyverse); library(haven); library(tidysynth)   # or library(Synth)

tx <- read_dta("data/texas.dta")

out <- tx %>%
  synthetic_control(outcome = bmprison, unit = state, time = year,
                    i_unit = "Texas", i_time = 1993, generate_placebos = TRUE) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1985:1993, poverty = mean(poverty), income = mean(income)) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1988, bmprison_1988 = mean(bmprison)) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1990, bmprison_1990 = mean(bmprison), alcohol = mean(alcohol),
                     perc1519 = mean(perc1519)) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1991, bmprison_1991 = mean(bmprison)) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1992, bmprison_1992 = mean(bmprison)) %>%
  generate_predictor(time_window = 1990:1991, aidscapita = mean(aidscapita), black = mean(black)) %>%
  generate_weights(optimization_window = 1985:1993) %>%
  generate_control()

out %>% grab_unit_weights() %>% filter(weight > 0.01) %>% arrange(desc(weight))




A handful of donors with positive weight — in the Python fit, Florida ≈ 0.56, New York ≈ 0.27, Illinois ≈ 0.17, everyone else zero (the book’s Stata fit lands on California, Florida, Illinois and Louisiana; solver and predictor details move the weights, not the picture). That sparsity is what the constraints produce.



Step 2 — Plot Texas against synthetic Texas and the gap

PythonR


Z0, Z1 = dp.make_outcome_mats(time_period=range(1985, 2001))
path = pd.DataFrame({"Texas": Z1, "Synthetic Texas": Z0 @ synth.W})
path["gap"] = path["Texas"] - path["Synthetic Texas"]
print(path.round(0))

fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
path[["Texas", "Synthetic Texas"]].plot(ax=ax[0]); ax[0].axvline(1993, color="grey", ls="--")
path["gap"].plot(ax=ax[1]); ax[1].axhline(0, color="grey"); ax[1].axvline(1993, color="grey", ls="--")
ax[0].set_ylabel("Black male prisoners"); ax[1].set_ylabel("Texas − synthetic"); plt.tight_layout()


out %>% plot_trends()
out %>% plot_differences()




Pre-1993 the two series track closely (pre-period RMSPE ≈ 900 prisoners on a base of 15,000–29,000). From 1994 the gap opens to ≈ +10,000 and then ≈ +20,000–27,000 per year from 1995 on, averaging ≈ 23,000 over 1994–2000: Texas holds roughly 23,000 more Black men in prison than its synthetic twin predicts. Check the pre-period RMSPE before believing any of it.



Step 3 — Placebo-in-space inference

PythonR


def fit_state(st):
    d = Dataprep(foo=tx, dependent="bmprison", unit_variable="statefip", time_variable="year",
                 treatment_identifier=st, controls_identifier=[s for s in tx.statefip.unique() if s != st],
                 predictors=["poverty", "income"], predictors_op="mean", time_predictors_prior=range(1985, 1994),
                 special_predictors=dp.special_predictors, time_optimize_ssr=range(1985, 1994))
    s = Synth(); s.fit(dataprep=d, optim_method="BFGS", optim_initial="ols")
    Z0, Z1 = d.make_outcome_mats(time_period=range(1985, 2001)); g = Z1 - Z0 @ s.W
    pre  = np.sqrt((g.loc[1985:1993] ** 2).mean())
    post = np.sqrt((g.loc[1994:2000] ** 2).mean())
    return pd.Series({"pre_rmspe": pre, "post_rmspe": post, "ratio": post / pre})

# This loop fits 51 synthetic controls and takes several minutes.
placebo = pd.DataFrame({names[st]: fit_state(st) for st in tx.statefip.unique()}).T
placebo = placebo.sort_values("ratio", ascending=False)
print(placebo.head(10).round(1))
rank = int((placebo.index == "Texas").argmax()) + 1
print(f"Texas rank: {rank} of {len(placebo)}  ->  p = {rank/len(placebo):.3f}")


out %>% plot_placebos()
out %>% plot_mspe_ratio()
out %>% grab_signficance()      # (sic) returns the rank-based p-value




Texas has the largest post/pre RMSPE ratio of all 51 units: ≈ 25.9, against 20.4 for the runner-up (Illinois) and single digits for most states. The rank-based \(p = 1/51 ≈\) 0.02. The placebo-gap plot shows Texas’s line leaving the band of 50 grey placebo lines after 1993. The book’s convention is to drop placebos whose pre-period RMSPE is more than some multiple of the treated unit’s; here only one state exceeds twice Texas’s, so the result does not depend on it.



Step 4 — Wrap-up: which design, when
Put three fresh questions to the room and make the group pick a design and name its key assumption and its first diagnostic. Suggested questions:

Did a city’s new minimum-wage ordinance reduce restaurant employment? — DiD or synthetic control against comparable cities; parallel trends / pre-period fit; event-study leads or placebo-in-space.
Does an extra year of schooling raise earnings for students who barely pass a school-entry test? — RDD on the test score; continuity at the cutoff; density test and covariate smoothness.
Do defendants assigned public defenders get longer sentences than those with private counsel? — Selection on unobservables is severe; an instrument such as random assignment of public-defender availability (judge-leniency style); relevance and exclusion; first-stage F and a complier description.

Then the decision tree, in words. If treatment was randomized, compare means and use randomization inference. If selection is on observables you can defend with a DAG, match or weight, and check overlap. If treatment switches at a threshold, RD. If something exogenous shifts treatment but not the outcome, IV, and say whose effect you are estimating. If you observe units before and after a change, fixed effects or DiD, with an event study to show the pre-period. If you have one treated aggregate and a long pre-period, synthetic control with placebo inference. If none of those apply, the honest answer is that the data cannot answer the causal question, and that is a finding.

title: Session 9 · Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
Exercises

Leave-one-out. Drop Florida (the largest-weight donor) from the donor pool and refit the synthetic Texas. How much do the weights and the post-period gap change? Then also drop the state with the next-largest weight. What does sensitivity to a single donor tell you?
Placebo-in-time. Pretend treatment happened in 1989 and fit the synthetic control using only 1985–1988 to choose weights. Is there a spurious “effect” after 1989? Why is this a useful check in addition to placebo-in-space?
Design memo. Pick a causal question from your own work. In one page: state the estimand (ATE, ATT, LATE, local effect at a cutoff…), the design you would use, its identifying assumption written as a counterfactual statement, two diagnostics you would show, and the one thing that would make you abandon the design.

title: Session 9 · Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
Solutions






Solutions (click to expand)





1. Without Florida the weight shifts to Illinois (0.44), New York (0.35) and California (0.21); the post-period gap is ≈ 23,600 and the pre-RMSPE rises only slightly (≈ 1,050). Dropping New York as well leaves Illinois 0.56 / California 0.44, a gap of ≈ 23,000 and pre-RMSPE ≈ 1,250. The result is not an artifact of any one donor. Large sensitivity to one donor would mean the synthetic unit was really a single comparison state, and you would be back to a one-control DiD.
2. With a 1989 pseudo-treatment, the synthetic and actual series continue to track through 1993, with no gap that resembles the post-1993 one. Placebo-in-time guards against the pre-period fit being achieved by overfitting a short window; placebo-in-space guards against the post-period gap being within the range of ordinary noise.
3. Discussed in the meeting. A good memo names the counterfactual explicitly (“absent the ordinance, employment in city A would have followed the trend in cities B–D”).

title: Session 9 · Synthetic control, and which design when
text:
Facilitator notes






Facilitator notes (click to expand)





Run Step 3 before the meeting. The 51-fit placebo loop takes several minutes in Python; have the results table ready and only re-run the Texas fit live. tidysynth with generate_placebos = TRUE does the loop inside generate_weights().
Misconception: the weights are “the” comparison states. They are the solution to an optimization with the predictors you chose. Change the predictors and the weights move (Step 1’s expect box shows this between implementations). What should not move much is the post-period gap.
Misconception: a pre-period fit that looks good is good enough. Insist on the pre-RMSPE number and the placebo-in-time check. Synthetic control with a short or badly fitted pre-period is a very elaborate way of picking a control state by hand.
Wrap-up block. Give it the full 15 minutes. It is the only time in the series the group practices choosing a design rather than executing one, and it is the skill the book is actually teaching.
Where to go next. The book’s own “Mixtape Sessions” workshops; Causal Inference for the Brave and True (Python-first, free); Huntington-Klein’s The Effect (free, R and Python, with the causaldata package); and the 2021–2023 DiD literature (Goodman-Bacon; Callaway & Sant’Anna; Sun & Abraham; de Chaisemartin & D’Haultfœuille; Roth et al.’s survey).
Discussion prompts. (a) Why is a synthetic control with 50 donors and 9 pre-years not simply overfitting? (b) What is the estimand here — ATT for Texas — and why can it not be generalized to other states?

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Last time

Regression anatomy: “controlling for” is mechanical
The open question: which variables should you control for?
Regression cannot answer that. A DAG can.

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
DAG grammar

Nodes are variables; \(A \to B\) means \(A\) causes \(B\)
A missing arrow is a strong claim: no direct effect
The graph encodes what you believe before looking at data
Acyclic: no variable causes itself

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Paths

A path is any sequence of edges between \(D\) and \(Y\), ignoring direction
Backdoor path: starts with an arrow into \(D\) — carries non-causal association
A path is blocked if it contains

a non-collider you condition on, or
a collider you do not condition on

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Confounder vs collider


Confounder \(D \leftarrow X \to Y\)

Open by default
Conditioning on \(X\) closes it


Collider \(D \to C \leftarrow Y\)

Closed by default
Conditioning on \(C\) opens it

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
The backdoor criterion
\(X\) identifies the effect of \(D\) on \(Y\) if

\(X\) blocks every backdoor path from \(D\) to \(Y\), and
\(X\) contains no descendant of \(D\)


The set can be empty (randomization)
Everything in Sessions 4 and 7 is a bet that some \(X\) satisfies this

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
The discrimination DAG

female → discrimination → occupation → wage
discrimination → wage (direct)
ability → occupation, ability → wage (unobserved)
“Control for occupation” sounds careful. Occupation is a collider on discrimination → occupation ← ability → wage.

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Walkthrough

Simulate the DAG; three regressions, three answers
Trace every path and classify each node
Talent and beauty among movie stars: selection is conditioning

dagitty finds the adjustment set for you

title: Directed acyclic graphs
text:
Takeaway

More controls are not safer. The right adjustment set comes from the graph, and the graph comes from theory and institutional knowledge — not from the data.

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Last time

SDO = ATE + selection bias + HTE bias
Randomization kills both. Without it?
Today’s bet: we can see everything that drives selection

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Conditional independence
\[(Y^0, Y^1) \perp D \mid X\]

Within strata of \(X\), treatment is as good as random
The backdoor criterion, in potential-outcomes clothing
Untestable: it is a claim about unobservables

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Common support
\[0 < P(D = 1 \mid X) < 1\]

Every covariate profile needs both treated and untreated units
Without it you are extrapolating, not matching
The one assumption you can check — so check it

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Subclassification

Stratify on \(X\); difference in means within each stratum
Average with the treated group’s stratum shares → ATT
Works with 2–3 discrete covariates
Dies of the curse of dimensionality immediately after

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
The propensity score

\(p(X) = P(D = 1 \mid X)\)
Rosenbaum & Rubin: if CIA holds given \(X\), it holds given \(p(X)\)
One number replaces the whole vector
Estimate with a logit; then stratify, weight (IPW), or match on it

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Not a prediction problem

You are not trying to predict treatment well
A score with perfect separation means no overlap
The goal is covariate balance, and the diagnostic is the balance table

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Dehejia–Wahba

NSW experiment: training raised 1978 earnings by ≈ $1,800
Replace the experimental controls with CPS: −$8,500
Propensity-score methods with the right covariates and overlap: back to ≈ $1,800–2,000
Matching can work. It can also fail silently.

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Walkthrough

Titanic: raw gap 0.35 → subclassified 0.24
NSW vs CPS: the −$8,500 disaster
Estimate the score; look at the histogram
IPW on the overlap region; nearest-neighbor ATT

title: Matching and subclassification
text:
Takeaway

Matching is a bet that the DAG has no unobserved confounder. The propensity score makes the bet tractable; overlap and balance are the only things you can verify.

title: Instrumental variables
text:
Last time

A fuzzy RD: treatment probability jumps at the cutoff
Effect = jump in \(Y\) / jump in \(D\)
That is an IV. Today: any variable can play the cutoff’s role

title: Instrumental variables
text:
The problem

\(Y = \alpha + \delta D + u\) with \(\mathrm{Cov}(D, u) \neq 0\)
If \(Z\) moves \(D\) and is otherwise unrelated to \(Y\):

\[\delta_{IV} = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(Z, Y)}{\mathrm{Cov}(Z, D)} = \frac{\text{reduced form}}{\text{first stage}}\]

title: Instrumental variables
text:
Three conditions (plus one)



Condition
Meaning
Testable?




Relevance
\(Z\) predicts \(D\)
Yes — first-stage F


Exclusion
\(Z \to Y\) only through \(D\)
No


Independence
\(Z\) as good as random w.r.t. \(u\)
No


Monotonicity
No defiers
No

title: Instrumental variables
text:
2SLS

Regress \(D\) on \(Z\) and covariates; keep \(\hat{D}\)
Regress \(Y\) on \(\hat{D}\) and the same covariates
Use an IV routine for the SEs — two lm calls get them wrong

title: Instrumental variables
text:
Weak instruments

Weak first stage → 2SLS biased toward OLS, badly behaved
Rule of thumb: F > 10; be nervous below 20
Prefer just-identified models; always report the F

title: Instrumental variables
text:
LATE

With heterogeneous effects, IV identifies the effect for compliers: units whose \(D\) is moved by \(Z\)
Different instruments → different compliers → different LATEs
Card’s compliers: people for whom college distance was binding
Stevenson’s compliers: defendants detained by a strict judge, released by a lenient one

title: Instrumental variables
text:
Walkthrough

Card: OLS return to schooling ≈ 0.07
First stage (0.33) and reduced form (0.04) by hand → Wald ≈ 0.12
2SLS with proper SEs
Judge leniency: OLS 0.035 vs 2SLS 0.16

title: Instrumental variables
text:
Takeaway

IV is reduced form over first stage. Relevance you can test; exclusion you must argue; and the answer is a LATE for whoever the instrument moves.

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Last time

The 2×2: no standard errors, no test of parallel trends
Today: many periods, many groups — and a new problem

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Event studies

Replace \(\text{Treat} \times \text{Post}\) with \(\text{Treat} \times \text{Year}_t\) for every \(t\) (omit one)
Leads (pre-treatment) should be ≈ 0
Lags trace the dynamic effect
Flat leads make parallel trends plausible; they do not prove it

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Placebos and triple differences

If theory says the effect exists only for a group / cohort / window, estimate it where it should not and demand zero
DDD: subtract the placebo group’s DD from the treated group’s DD
Absorbs group-specific shocks a plain DD would call “treatment”

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Abortion legalization (Cunningham & Cornwell 2013)

Five states repealed bans in 1970; Roe in 1973
Treated cohorts: born 1971–73 in repeal states
Prediction: lower gonorrhea among 15–19 year olds in 1986–92, tracing a parabola as the cohort ages through the bracket
Placebo: 25–29 year olds

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Staggered adoption

Units treated at different times; TWFE: \(Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \delta D_{it} + e_{it}\)
Goodman-Bacon: \(\hat{\delta}\) is a weighted average of every 2×2 in the data
Including late-treated vs already-treated as “control”
If effects grow over time, those 2×2s are biased — sometimes to the wrong sign

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Modern estimators

Callaway–Sant’Anna: ATT for each cohort × period, using only never- or not-yet-treated controls; aggregate with chosen weights
Sun–Abraham: the same idea inside an interaction-weighted event-study regression
Both need a clean control group; neither is magic

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Castle doctrine (Cheng & Hoekstra 2013)

“Stand your ground” laws, 2005–2010, 21 states
TWFE: log homicide up ≈ 8%
29 never-treated states → the decomposition puts 90% of weight on clean comparisons

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Walkthrough

Abortion event study: the parabola
Placebo cohort and DDD
Castle TWFE
Bacon decomposition by hand; a modern estimator

title: Difference-in-differences, deep dive
text:
Takeaway

The event-study plot is the deliverable. TWFE is a weighted average with weights you did not choose; decompose it, and if the forbidden comparisons carry weight, use an estimator that refuses to make them.
